speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: RATE OF INFLATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the disheartening response of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) to the question of the government's plans to combat record inflation prospects facing our country, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Portage (Mr. Masniuk):
That this House reject the only stated government policy, namely, that Canadians should henceforth cease eating, drinking, lighting, heating or cooling their homes in order to bring down the rate of inflation to the level projected in the last budget of the Minister of Finance.

subsubtopic: AIR SERVICE TO WESTERN CANADA-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I request permission to move a motion under Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the promise made by the Prime Minister during the 1974 election of early action to provide a first-class air service to western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan in the interests of economic growth, and in view of the press release of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) on January 31, 1977, requesting applications from carriers to provide commuter air service and jet service to these areas, and the application of Great Lakes Airlines to provide the necessary jet service now before the air transport committee, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ritchie):
That the minister use his good offices to urge the air transport committee to reach a decision on the application at the earliest possible date, particularly in light of the air transportation requirements of the Canada Winter Games to be held in Brandon next February.

subsubtopic: BEEF IMPORTS-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Last Friday, the U.S. announced that beef imports to that country will be increased by 16 per cent. As a result of the American move, Canadian beef markets have already fallen by 10 per cent. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin):
That the Minister of Agriculture assure this House that the government will not increase beef imports but, rather, will adopt measures to bring about self-sufficiency in the Canadian beef industry.

subsubtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF PRAIRIE RAIL AUTHORITY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. On Tuesday last, Mr. Justice Emmett Hall told the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, "The task that was committed to the Prairie Rail Action Committee was premature and impossible of fulfilment within the time-frame given that committee". He also said PRAC recommendation to abandon the portion of the rail line from Liberty to Dilke was "a serious mistake". Therefore, before the Prairie Rail Action Committee can do any more damage to the grain handling system, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom):
That this House request the government to require the Minister of Transport to reject PRAC abandonment recommendations to date, to disband the PRAC, and to bring forward legislation to set up the prairie rail authority as recommended by the Hall royal commission.

subsubtopic: STATUS OF MIKHAIL KVATOV-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent necessity concerning evidence presented by the Crown at the preliminary trial of Peter Worthington under the Official Secrets Act several years ago; specifically, a statement by RCMP witness Spooner that Soviet diplomat Mikhail Kvatov was a KGB agent involved in certain activities from 1975 to 1976, the revelation of which by Mr. Worthington in the Toronto Sun allegedly prejudiced the security of the state. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie):
That the Solicitor General explain to the House the complete inconsistency between the RCMP testimony and information given on request to the member for Leeds by the RCMP during the week of June 3, 1975, with regard to the same Mikhail Kvatov stating that he was a bona fide diplomat and was not engaged in KGB activities and, finally, that the minister confirm whether or not the court was lied to by the RCMP or whether the member for Leeds was lied to.

subsubtopic: OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. It is based on very unhappy statistics brought out by Statistics Canada last week indicating that the exodus of capital from Canada continues, $335 million having been invested by Canadians abroad in that quarter alone, resulting in an outflow of capital in the 90-day period of over $3 million a day. Is the Minister of Finance aware of these figures? Does he find this exodus of capital alarming and, if so, would he give some explanation to the House and the people of Canada as to why this is occurring? I might add that over $1 billion has gone out in the last 12 months.

subsubtopic: OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the policy of the government is to let capital flow inside and outside of the country, we do not want to impose exchange controls. In order to have a lot of foreign capital in our economy, we must allow Canadians to make their own decisions about their investments. However, we are looking at the situation and watching it very carefully.

subsubtopic: OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is, again, to the Minister of Finance. It is obvious from the figures, which the minister does not deny, that the international community is now judging Canada as an unprofitable place in which to invest. Would the minister indicate whether he plans any steps to make the Canadian investment climate a little more attractive, so that needed capital for this country's development might start flowing in, instead of going out as has been the case?

subsubtopic: OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Canada has always been recognized as a good place for investment. A tremendous amount of money enters the country regularly, and we have the best illustration in the articles published last week which indicated that U.S. bankers who established a $3 billion line of credit for Canada said that if we had wanted more it would have been possible to obtain it.

subsubtopic: OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance does not see the difference between raising debt funds to cover current
Oral Questions
account expenses of his government and needed capital that is not coming into the country. Is there an industrial strategy in place in this country to which the minister can refer us, and is there an industrial strategy that the world can see because, frankly, it is a very confusing picture? We have the Export Development Corporation financing pulp mills and steel mills to compete with Canada's in future years. We even have Petro-Can planning a $500 million investment to heighten the outflow of capital still further. Do we have an industrial strategy?

subsubtopic: OUTFLOW OF CAPITAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are working very intensely on that. I do not know if the hon. member is aware, but I discussed that matter very thoroughly last February with the premiers of the provinces. As a result of the February conference, studies are being made in order to elaborate the strategy in every sector of the Canadian economy. We have made a lot of progress in that regard. In terms of the difference between debt and equity investment in Canada, a lot of people in Canada were complaining for a hell of a long time that there was too much equity coming in and not enough debt financing.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. There is a grand total, including bonds, short and long-term investment, of $18 million in investment capital leaving Canada daily. The Conference Board recently reported that 26 Canadian Firms have made major investments in the United States. That is a clear indication that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce has completely failed in his portfolio: he cannot attract business here and he does nothing to keep in Canada those already here. Can the minister explain to the House why these 26 Canadian firms are investing in the United States?

Mr. Speaker, if you look at the figures, you will see that since the beginning of 1978 the balance of payments in trade in Canada is in favour of Canada: it is increasing from year to year. Three years ago we had a deficit in trade balance; with the trend this year, we will have a trade balance in favour of Canada of more than $5 billion. That means we must be doing something right. We are one of the few nations which can claim such a favourable trade balance in favour of its own economy.

Perhaps the minister can explain why they are not consulting firms such as John Labatt Limited, which has announced plans for a wheat-starch and gluten facility in South Carolina, and the St. Laurence Steel and Wire Company which has leased facilities in New York state and will produce hockey masks. Will the Minister of Finance make inquiries, as the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce is obviously not doing anything to keep these firms here. Why can these hockey masks not be made in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I do not have to defend the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce: he can defend himself very well. I just pointed out the great balance in terms

June 15, 1978
Oral Questions
of trade for Canada. It is improving from month to month. That is certainly due to the fact that we have a very good Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources regarding the struggle which is going on between Petro-Can and Occidental Petroleum Company of Los Angeles, each seeking to acquire a controlling interest in Husky Oil Company of Calgary. If the government follows its previous practice, this matter will not be referred to parliament but dealt with by FIRA and then by cabinet. Members of this House may find some day that this great asset has been transferred to the control of a foreign company. I ask the minister whether he is prepared, either today or on motions tomorrow, to make a statement to the House concerning the negotiations which are in progress and the intentions of the government with respect to a matter which he himself said in the House the other day was of national interest.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: I am sure there will be opportunities during the question period from day to day to answer questions such as those put forward by the hon. member today and on previous occasions. I shall be pleased to bring hon. members up to date on events as they may unfold. With respect to making any more formal or lengthy statement, I am not planning one at the present time-it might be premature-but, as I say, I would be pleased to answer specific questions.

I think the House is entitled to a statement of the government's intentions. The minister knows perfectly well that Husky controls more than 1.5 million acres of proven oil reserves on the Alberta-Saskatchewan border and that by using new technology it has a possibility of recovering 16 billion barrels of heavy crude oil. This is of great importance to Canada in a period when our light oil is being phased out.
Is the minister prepared to give specific assurances to the House that the government will take whatever steps are necessary to ensure that the control of Husky Oil Company and of its assets will continue to be maintained in Canada either by Petro-Canada or by Petro-Canada in partnership with the governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
As I have said in the House in the last few days and on many occasions in the past, development of the heavy oils of western Canada, particularly those of Saskatchewan, is very much a national priority. Indeed, at a meeting of first ministers, the Premier of Saskatchewan and the Prime Minister addressed themselves to this question. One of the

results of that meeting was a commitment to move forward with the development of this heavy oil. We have regarded the takeover bid by Petro-Canada as being fully consistent with the priority we have assigned for the development of this heavy oil. Petro-Canada decided on the takeover route because its officials had reached the conclusion, as a result of negotiations and discussions with Husky Oil in the preceding months, that they would not be able to bring this oil-rich land into production for the benefit of Canada and Canadians. That is why Petro-Canada has gone forward with the blessing of the federal government.
If, as a result of the offer by the Occidental group, development of this heavy oil would be in every way guaranteed, one would have to come to the conclusion, it seems to me, that a Canadian objective had been secured. For this reason, I do not wish to prejudge either offer at the present time. The offer has been put forward in good faith by Petro-Canada. The president of Petro-Canada has told me his organization intends to proceed with this offer. What further action the consortium of Husky and Occidental may take, I am not in a position to forecast, nor am I in a position to speculate-
Order.

May I
direct a final supplementary to the Prime Minister? Can the Prime Minister tell us the policy of the government with respect to this matter? We have just heard the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources say that the acquisition of Husky is in the national interest. The press quotes the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce as saying, "I am not shedding any tears over Petro-Canada". He says Petro-Canada can go out and buy land and put up a refinery of its own.
What is the policy with respect to this matter? There have been conflicting statements from two ministers and I think the House and the country are entitled to know whether the Prime Minister, as head of the government of this country, is prepared to commit himself to saying that this tremendous economic asset will be retained under the control of Canadians and preferably under the control of the federal government and the two provincial governments involved.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
With respect, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member either misunderstood or misinterpreted the answer of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. He did not say it was in the national interest that the acquisition by Petro-Canada move ahead. He said it was in the national interest that these heavy oils and the freehold land under which the oils lay be exploited. He was quite clear in indicating that Petro-Canada was seeking that, and if somebody else was seeking that, that would also be in the national interest.
June 15, 1978

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Statistics Canada has just reported that railway car loadings, which are an accurate measurement of industrial activity, decreased by 7 per cent during the first five months of this year compared with the same period a year ago, and that Canadian industry is operating at only 82.7 per cent of its capacity, the lowest point it has reached in three years-and it is going down. Would the minister advise the House, either now or on motions tomorrow, what plans he has to turn this very serious situation around and restore Canadian industry to a healthy condition?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have in progress right now a number of distinct measures which will assist Canadian industry a great deal. While Canadian industry might well be operating at 85 per cent capacity-

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: It is 82.7 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: It is 82.7 per cent, then, I am not going to argue about the figure. What I am saying is that we must be realistic. Part of that industry is always under repair and all of it is not capable of producing at 100 per cent capacity at all times. I think the House should bear that fact in mind.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, It has been made very obvious that the minister has no plans to turn around this very serious situation. Has he nothing better to offer than his present plan for helping Canadian industry, that of reducing import tariffs by an average of 40 per cent against all products coming into this country which compete with Canadian industrial products on the Canadian market which, if allowed to take place, will make competition for our Canadian industries far more difficult on the Canadian market and will increase unemployment very materially indeed?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought the hon. member was aware of the things we were doing to help Canadian industry. We have set up 22 sector studies which encompass management, labour, provincial governments, the federal government, retailers and importers. These 22 sector studies will result in reports by the end of this month. We hope to make the reports public by about the third week in July. They will be submitted to a national board which will make a coherent effort on behalf of industry to make a presentation to the first ministers' conference.
With respect to tariff negotiations, I am amazed at the negativism-I really should not be amazed, after the months I have listened to hon. members opposite-in the hon. member's suggestion that a reduction of tariffs will hurt Canadian industry. A reduction of tariffs will broaden Canadian industries' marketability around the world. We have 23 million people, but there are 200 million people immediately south of us, so if our Canadian industry has a better opportunity to get
Oral Questions
into that larger market we will enhance opportunities for Canadian industries.

subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, these problems have been with us for several years. Long before now the government should have had a concrete plan for turning around this very serious situation. Does the minister not realize that the time for setting up boards, commissions and studies and more boards, commissions and studies has long passed and that we should have been getting action long before now to get the economy of this country rolling?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MEASURES TO IMPROVE PRODUCTIVITY
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for St. John's West.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. In the last quarter of last year, Canadian industry operated at a rate of 84 per cent utilization. It is down to 82.7 per cent this quarter, the worst since 1961. Last spring the minister said that Canada's economy would be a lot healthier next spring, that the devalued dollar would begin to be felt and the devaluation would give the manufacturing industry room to breathe. How is it that the minister's forecast is not accurate and that, instead, Canadian manufacturing is in its worst state since 1961? What emergency measures is the minister taking, apart altogether from studies and task forces?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not agree, and I do not think the House should agree-certainly, Canadians should not agree-that our industry is in as terrible a shape as opposition members make it out to be. We have had a continuous merchandising trade surplus for the last 17 months.
Selling our resources.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Selling resources? Let me tell the House that 10 per cent of our total exports are agricultural goods, 20 per cent are oil, gas and minerals, and 66% per cent are manufactured and semi-processed goods.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We are becoming a large industrialized nation and we are doing very well at it because we have built up a trade surplus in the past 17 months. In retrospect, if one looks at the United States, one finds that they have had a merchandising trade deficit for the last 32 months. So we are doing very well.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian industry has so much room to breathe that it is not even operating. Last fall,

June 15, 1978
Oral Questions
in November, the Economic Council of Canada said that we faced five years of high unemployment, continuing inflation, modest growth and a large deficit in international payments. The minister said then that the council probably did not have all the available information at its disposal when it was doing its forecast and that it was wrong, it was too pessimistic. subsubtopic: NOISE LEVELS IN AREA OF TORONTO AIRPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport who I understand is aware of the concern over the controversial proposal to build a 450-unit housing development beside Centennial Park in Etobicoke, just to the south of Toronto international airport. In view of the fact that provincial approval to build the units was based on the hypothetical noise exposure forecast figures produced by the minister's department, will the minister order his officials to conduct on-site testing, financed by the federal government, of the actual noise levels in order to ensure that local and provincial authorities are in possession of up to date, accurate information about noise levels in the area?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: NOISE LEVELS IN AREA OF TORONTO AIRPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will certainly take the suggestion under consideration. I have already asked my officials to do a further analysis of the noise situation and of the impact upon the airport of any possible further housing development in that area. I also hold the fairly strong personal view that such development is rather inadvisable notwithstanding what the technical situation may be with regard to the noise contours and location of the houses, because from knowledge in the past it has been clear that where housing has developed near an airport there is later increased pressure to decrease the usefulness of the airport and the great investment we have in it. Accordingly, I am today writing to Mr. Snow to this effect.

subsubtopic: NOISE LEVELS IN AREA OF TORONTO AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his answer and ask whether or not he is aware of the proposal that has been made by Alderman Dick O'Brien, of Etobicoke, that the federal government will do as is done in other instances around federal airports, which is to purchase the land which would be used for this housing development and contribute it

to the borough of Etobicoke as an extension to Centennial Park upon which it abuts. Is the minister giving serious consideration to that proposal?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subsubtopic: NOISE LEVELS IN AREA OF TORONTO AIRPORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, kept me fully aware of all opinions and events in this area. I think it may be seen as a fair division of responsibility if we, as the federal government, involved in investments in major airports put those investments in place and that the local people should make a contribution with regard to zoning.

So, Mr. Speaker, to get back to the very serious question of the hon. member for Windsor West, let me say that we have assurances that there is no excess profit gouging or profiteering in the food retailing or processing industry. But of course, as the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs said yesterday, we are looking into the matter and we are making sure that our information is correct and continues to be correct.
As to improving the situation, the minister said yesterday that we hope in the weeks to come to make any announcements which will become government policy.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The new monitoring agency announced today by the Economic Council of Canada to take over during the post-control period will not have the investigatory authority that the Food Prices Review Board had under the Inquiries Act. Would the Prime Minister tell the House how this monitoring agency can function effectively in the marketplace if it does not have this investigatory authority, and whether or not the agency will, as did the Food Prices Review Board, report publicly or to the cabinet?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: If the hon. member refers to the letter which was made public this morning by the chairman of the Economic Council of Canada, I believe he will have the answer to both those questions. In the case of inquiries under the Inquiries Act or in any other form, the answer is that in areas where the Economic Council of Canada's special commission finds that a special inquiry is called for, it will so recommend to the government, which will then act in one way or another under the present legislation or by putting another proposal before the House. 1 believe that covers the question asked by the hon. member.

Members of the House have not received a copy of the release this morning and hence we do not have the advantage which the Prime Minister has. Is he saying to the House that the new monitoring agency will only be able to operate after the fact-in other words, they can only recommend an inquiry after the fact-as opposed to being able to move in and identify abuses which are taking place in the marketplace? Is that the position of the new board and, if so, how can it operate effectively and do a job in monitoring the marketplace?

Yes, it is after the fact and it is with material which is readily available publicly. Power has not been given to this new body to carry out investigations or to call witnesses on
Oral Questions
its own. I might remind the hon. member that this government, early this session, put legislation before the House to set up a post-AIB monitoring board. We heard great argument from all sides but particularly from the Tory party that they did not want to support it. In particular, at the first ministers' conference in February, a majority of the provinces indicated that they did not want, and would not support, the initiatives for post-controls of the Minister of Finance. As a result of that, we accepted a compromise, which was moved forward by the provinces, that we would make a request to the Economic Council. That request was made and the Economic Council studied the matter. The answer is given in a letter which was made public this morning at a press conference by Mrs. Ostry and equally, I believe, it was made public by my office.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It is in the area of prices and concerns the kickbacks which are being made to Dominion Stores and other companies in Ontario as revealed by a special committee of the Ontario legislature. Now we have evidence that at least one dairy is giving a 26 per cent kickback to Dominion Stores in fluid milk, a canned food processor gives a rebate or a kickback of some 10 per cent to Dominion Stores, and a kickback of some 15 per cent on vegetables by some chain stores as well as 10 per cent on apples.
In view of the fact that this will result in rapid concentration and that some stores are now paying more at the wholesale level for their commodities than the large supermarkets are at the retail level, can the minister indicate if he has had a chance to investigate this entire area of kickbacks by processors, and so on, to the chain stores? If he has not had a chance to look at it, what will he do?

speakeroldname: Hon. Warren Allmand (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I said approximately a week ago, this matter has been under examination by the director of investigation and research under the combines act. According to the combines act, if these rebates were offered to all stores on an equal basis, then they would be legal. However, if the evidence indicates, as the hon. member states, that there is discrimination in the offering of rebates, then of course it would be illegal and the director could take legal action against them. At one point we did not have that evidence, but if evidence has now come in, then of course it would be illegal under the combines act and action can be taken.

Mr. Speaker, there is at least one case where the kickback from canned food processors to Dominion Stores is at least 10 per cent greater than it is to A and P. Therefore, I assume that is illegal and the minister will take action. I can provide him with that evidence.
I should like to direct a question to the Acting Minister of National Revenue, the Minister of National Health and Welfare. Testimony before an Ontario committee indicated that

June 15, 1978
Oral Questions
Loblaws' rebates are paid out in part to a separate company called Intersave, a name which I think is quite appropriate for Loblaws. In view of the fact that supermarket profits are already high-for example, in the case of Safeway, up 61 per cent and in the case of Loeb, up 163 per cent-can the minister indicate if her department has investigated these kickbacks? Can she assure us that chain stores are not using this method of kickback in order to evade taxes which are otherwise due to the Canadian people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will transmit to the Department of National Revenue the allegations of eventual tax evasion by the companies the hon. member referred to.

subsubtopic: POLITICAL CLEARANCE OF MAJOR CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. On Monday, the hon. member for Central Nova questioned the Minister of Finance who was the Acting Prime Minister at the time. His questions concerned a meeting which was held some time ago between the present Minister of National Defence and the chairman of the National Capital Commission wherein the following quotation appeared:
The minister (meaning the present Minister of National Defence) wants to make sure that the firms chosen for major contracts of this sort are cleared politically with the ministers responsible through this office.
Can the minister tell the House if that quotation still represents his method of handling bids for government contracts?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: POLITICAL CLEARANCE OF MAJOR CONTRACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the context of that particular quotation, which I do not recall, it accurately reflects my position. It was not on bids. Of course, bids always go to the lowest bidder unless there are exceptional circumstances.

subsubtopic: POLITICAL CLEARANCE OF MAJOR CONTRACTS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: POLITICAL CLEARANCE OF MAJOR CONTRACTS
speechtext: We are talking about contracts for professional services. I would always consult the regional minister in an area to make certain all the contracts which do not go by tender are distributed properly and do not all go to one company in a region, and to ensure that ample opportunity is given to smaller companies in different parts of the region, smaller communities and disadvantaged areas, in order for them to take full advantage of it, rather than the traditional firms which might have very close connections in the public service. 1 think it is up to ministers to fulfil their responsibilities to see that there is proper distribution of contracts throughout an area and that all companies have an opportunity, particularly when there are no bids.

subsubtopic: POLITICAL CLEARANCE OF MAJOR CONTRACTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the procedures for awarding the contract for the new fighter aircraft entail the Minister of

National Defence taking the final selection of his department to cabinet. If the five firms involved are to be screened in any way to determine their political clearance, does the minister not believe an undue advantage will accrue to that firm which has on its board of directors the former minister of finance, the Hon. Donald Macdonald? Has the minister issued any directives to ensure that his former colleague will not exert any influence whatsoever on the decision?

subsubtopic: POLITICAL CLEARANCE OF MAJOR CONTRACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all, there are a whole number of factors involved in that decision and no political influence in that sense would be exercised. If it was the purpose of MacDonnell-Douglas to get one of the finest directors on its board that it could choose from among Canadians. They have achieved that purpose. If that company believes it is helping them to get a contract, of course they have made a mistake because they would be underrating both the government and Mr. Macdonald.

subsubtopic: POLITICAL CLEARANCE OF MAJOR CONTRACTS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: POLITICAL CLEARANCE OF MAJOR CONTRACTS
speechtext: The fact of the matter is that he is a man of great integrity. I might say that he has had no contact with me on this matter since he went to that board of directors. The only effect it might have is that that company perhaps will have to prove itself 110 per cent, where the others have to prove themselves 100 per cent.

subsubtopic: POLITICAL CLEARANCE OF MAJOR CONTRACTS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: POLITICAL CLEARANCE OF MAJOR CONTRACTS
speechtext: You mean it does have an effect.

subsubtopic: POLITICAL CLEARANCE OF MAJOR CONTRACTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, does the Minister of National Defence actually believe that MacDonnell-Douglas took on Mr. Macdonald for his knowledge of aircraft, particularly fighter aircraft?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: POLITICAL CLEARANCE OF MAJOR CONTRACTS
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question, concerning youth and student employment, is directed to the right hon. Prime Minister in the absence of the Minister of Finance who is the chief economic minister. According to statistics which I have in my hands today issued by the government, 605,000 students will leave Canadian educational institutions in 1978 and become available to the labour force in 1978. Because of these unusually large statistics, can the Prime Minister tell us specifically what the government plans to do about it in terms of new initiatives to employ these young Canadians, in view of the general employment situation in Canada?
June 15, 1978

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in part an overwhelming proportion of these young Canadians will find jobs in the private sector.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: Tell them to leave the country.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: In so far as the others are concerned, just yesterday and the day before the Minister of Employment and Immigration gave figures to the hon. member and his colleagues indicating that a very high proportion, something like 30 per cent to 40 per cent, of government direct spending for job creation will be going to young Canadians.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the government is not reacting on the basis of these statistics today because they are based on the babies born in the post-war baby boom. In view of the very high rate of unemployment among students and young Canadians, and the very high statistics which the government has been well aware of for some time and informed us of today, can we not expect, without delay, some new and dynamic initiatives from the government to challenge the excellence of the younger generation?

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not suppose the hon. member, certainly not his party, is suggesting that the government be the employer of last resort for all Canadians. That is why I insist that the private sector is creating jobs, as has been made clear repeatedly in this House, at a rate which is substantially higher than that of any other industrialized society. The rate has been something like 300,000 jobs on a year over year basis. This is a higher rate than the 10-year historical average in Canada.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: Bunk.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: Someone over there says "bunk", Mr. Speaker, or something that sounded like that. I am not sure what this Latin word means in English, but I can tell him that the figures I am giving are the true figures.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: No, they are not.

subsubtopic: EMPLOYMENT OF YOUNG CANADIANS
speechtext: It serves no purpose, to the opposition or anyone, to say that this country and this economy are not creating jobs at a very high rate. They are, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS WITHIN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State. I am sure the minister is well aware of the developing impasse between the CBC staff announcers and management of a renegotiated contract which expired last July. In view of the conciliation report which was brought down earlier this week which, as I understand it, has been accepted by the announcers and rejected in part by the
Oral Questions
CBC management, and the report that there were over 250 violations of the previous contract during the last ten-year period by CBC management, has the minister expressed any concern to the president of the CBC, on behalf of the government, about the questionable industrial relations that exist within CBC management, or has he conferred with the Minister of Labour about possible violations of the Canada Labour Code?

subsubtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS WITHIN CORPORATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in a general way there are continuing discussions between myself and the president of the CBC about a variety of problems that exist in the corporation, including those of management and labour relations. As to the second part of the hon. member's question, there have not been specific discussions with the Minister of Labour to which he referred.

subsubtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS WITHIN CORPORATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the very high series of reported violations undei the previous contract, and the fact that there seem to be very real threats posed to present CBC staff announcers under the proposal brought forward, that they would adopt such a situation as a new category of short-term announcers with, seemingly, no particular benefit to the corporation, could the minister indicate whether, in view of one strike vote already being held by NABET and the possibility of another one next week, there will be any attempt made to have the CBC management adopt more appropriate industrial relations for a Crown corporation?

subsubtopic: LABOUR RELATIONS WITHIN CORPORATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows, I do not interfere directly in the management of the CBC; but I will be happy to do as I have in the past and bring his representations to the attention of management.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In view of press reports concerning the serious allegations of Mr. Arthur Porter, commissioner of the Ontario Royal Commission on Electric Power Planning, that information on the safety of nuclear generating plants was withheld from his commission by the Atomic Energy Control Board, has the minister investigated those allegations and can he assure the House that safety information of the Atomic Energy Control Board was not withheld from this royal commission?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have assured myself of those facts. I asked the president of the Atomic Energy Control Board what the allegations were based on and he told me he was not sure what they were. He then talked to Mr. Porter, the royal commissioner. I think the royal commissioner was perhaps under some misapprehension and had not realized, when he made his statement, that indeed the Atomic Energy Control

June 15, 1978
Oral Questions
Board had placed before the royal commission information of which the royal commissioner should have been aware. Subsequently, in a radio interview, the royal commissioner made a statement to the effect that he had erred in his judgment with respect to the words he had chosen and that, indeed, there was no risk with respect to the safety of Canadian nuclear reactors.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. He said a few minutes ago that Petro-Canada had the blessing of the Government of Canada with respect to its offer to Husky Oil. I would like to ask the minister whether Petro-Canada has secured the financial backing of the Government of Canada with respect to this offer which, as I understand it, amounts to something in excess of $500 million altogether and, if so, was this taken care of in the cash requirements put before the House at the time of the budget of the Minister of Finance?

speakeroldname: Hon. Aiastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the financial arrangements for the transaction, in the event that it is a successful bid, have been considered. Petro-Canada has negotiated a line of credit for the purposes of financing the greater part of the purchase. It would require some assistance from its capital budget which has already been submitted and approved, so there will be no additional funds provided to Petro-Canada by the federal government with respect to its over-all capital budget.

Mr. Speaker, with respect to the amount of capital it is anticipated that Petro-Canada would raise on its own, would this be raised by Petro-Canada without the guarantee and support of the Government of Canada? Is the minister saying, in effect, that this transaction would add nothing more to the cash requirements of the Government of Canada other than the amount already provided for in the budge as presented?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is precisely the fact.

subsubtopic: TARIFF ON EXPORTS TO EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I direct my question to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. In a statement released by the minister's department on June 13 concerning the results of ICNAF consultations in Bonn, we read that negotiators established reserves on several important stocks which will be allocated later either to Canadian fishermen or to other states in return for economic and commercial benefits offered by those states.
In light of that statement, and in view of the impact caused by the present boundary negotiations that are under way between Canada and the United States which reflect upon Canada's fishermen, plus their need for expanded markets, I

would ask the minister what kind of economic benefits he has in mind and what steps he has taken to secure the lowering of the 15 per cent tariff on Canadian fish when sold to the European Economic Community to a 3 per cent or 4 per cent level as charged by the Community to Norway and Iceland, for example, so that Canadian fishermen would at least have a fighting chance in those European markets.

speakeroldname: Hon. Rom6o LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
subsubtopic: TARIFF ON EXPORTS TO EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I notice that the hon. member did not mention our success in negotiating the prevention of countervailing with the U.S. authorities; but since he has not, I will. It was a very great victory for the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who in fact was able to demonstrate that we had separated the issue of countervailing and duties from the issue of boundaries. I recognize that hon. members opposite did, in fact, rejoice at the success.
With regard to the question asked by the hon. member, as he knows, quotas are being discussed for the year 1979. In some cases we expect Canadian fishermen to reach and even go beyond their quotas in the offshore fisheries and therefore there may be room for expansion in 1979. For that reason, we have kept some reserve for Canadian fishermen if they demonstrate that they can, in fact, take the additional quotas. The idea of commensurate benefit is exactly for the purpose expressed by the hon. member, namely, to gain access to markets. We are willing to say to certain nations which have vessels that are not sufficiently occupied or plants that are very short of supply, "if you offer us good access to your market, we will consider the possibility of offering some access to our zone".

subtopic: WHA SIGNING OF JUNIOR HOCKEY PLAYERS
WHA SIGNING OF JUNIOR HOCKEY PLAYERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport). It concerns the announcement today that three more under age junior hockey players are about to sign with the World Hockey Association, a clear violation not only of their own rules but of the minister's stated government policy that she opposes this kind of raiding of junior hockey. Can the minister advise the House what she proposes to do to stop what could be a state of anarchy existing in junior hockey if we continue to allow professional teams to sign under age players across Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Iona Campagnolo (Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
subtopic: WHA SIGNING OF JUNIOR HOCKEY PLAYERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to set up an inquiry into the non-professional levels of hockey as recommended in the all-party committee report on international hockey, chaired by Senator Buckwold. It is my intention to have that committee meet before the end of this month.
June 15, 1978

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subsubtopic: MR. McGRATH-ANSWER GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I know that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) would not deliberately mislead the House, and I know that he would want to correct the record in his reply to my question when he accused this House of opposing legislation to set up the regulatory monitoring agency to succeed the AntiInflation Board especially during the post-controls period. That, of course, is not true. I have checked with my House leader, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker), and with the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). They confirm what I knew anyway-that we did not oppose that proposition. I know the Prime Minister would not want to mislead the House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: MR. McGRATH-ANSWER GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, of course I accept the word of the hon. gentleman, but this is an interesting development. If the House would really prefer the act which had been proposed by the minister for the post inflation period, I wish we had heard about it before now. The difficulty in getting it through the House was precisely because we had been hearing it had not been accepted by the other side.

subsubtopic: MR. McGRATH-ANSWER GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: The minister said there was no act.

subsubtopic: MR. McGRATH-ANSWER GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
The minister said that he was prepared to move in the post inflation period with a special monitoring body. This was before the House for debate for quite some time-this was stated, if I recall correctly, in the Speech from the Throne. When we had the first ministers' conference it was indicated by the premiers that they preferred something else, and it is the something else that we have now, Mr. Speaker, the Economic Council of Canada.
If the hon. gentleman says they have not taken a position on that, I wish they had, because we would now have some other form of action.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. McGRATH-ANSWER GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext: Order, please. I see two other hon. members rising on points of order. The Minister for Public Works and Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Buchanan) has indicated his intention to participate in the question of privilege raised earlier by the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre). I wonder if I could take these points of order briefly, and then take the minister's intervention.

Mr. Speaker, a moment ago I raised a question with the hon. Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc). In his response the minister stated that he was somewhat surprised that we on this side had not referred to the agreement that had been reached on the countervailing duties proposed by the United States. In defence of my position I must say that we did not
Privilege-Mr. Stevens
raise the question of countervailing duties during the period that this matter was under discussion, at the expressed request of the minister. He stated to me personally that to raise this matter at such a delicate period in the negotiations between Canada and the United States could jeopardize those negotiations to the detriment of the interests of the Canadian fishing industry.
As the minister is well aware, the United States government has the right at any time to implement countervailing duties. It was only because he insisted or suggested that they would take away some of the assistance, namely, the two cents per pound paid to fishermen on October 1, that he was able to obtain agreement, so we are still in a very delicate situation with regard to the interests of Canadian fishermen.
I regret that the minister took what appeared to me to be an opportunity to make a cheap political attack on this side of the House when we had done everything possible to assist him in securing a rational and reasonable solution to what is, in my opinion, a very serious and very delicate problem.

speakeroldname: Hon. Romeo LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I offended the hon. member, I apologize. The fact is, in the preface to my answer to his question, I alluded to the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) whose heated exchange with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) is recorded in Hansard. He certainly showed signs of great nervousness at the possibility of countervail which, by the way, had been discussed for many, many months, and which had nothing to do with the present boundary difficulty.
I certainly recognize that the hon. member, in response to my request at one point, abstained from questioning in a delicate moment in our negotiations before this agreement was suspended, and for this I give him full credit. If I did have a complaint it was not with the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse), who has shown great responsibility in these matters, but it was possibly to make a point to the hon. member for St. John's West.

subsubtopic: MR. STEVENS-PRIME MINISTER'S REMARKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege arises from the remarks just made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he indicated some type of monitoring agency bill had been suggested to parliament and that the official opposition had somehow discouraged either its passage or introduction.
There is a great misunderstanding here, Mr. Speaker. Like my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), I would not say that the Prime Minister has deliberately misled the House. The fact is that a draft bill, some 30 or 40 pages long, calling for the setting up of a monitoring agency and extensive regulatory powers to be given

June 15, 1978
Business of the House
to the federal government, came into our possession, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) denied it categorically. He said there was no such legislation. He refused even to accept the draft I had in my hands, and in any event said he had no authority at all concerning such a bill and, if it had been drafted, it had not been done on his instructions. For the Prime Minister to indicate that the Minister of Finance was on the verge of introducing some such bill, is totally wrong.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. STEVENS-PRIME MINISTER'S REMARKS
speechtext: Order, please. Surely the point raised by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), further to that raised by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath), constitutes essentially a difference of opinion or a dispute as to interpretation between them and the Prime Minister of what he said. It does not constitute a question of privilege.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the business of the House. The government House leader has indicated the list of legislation on previous occasions. If the deputy House leader has anything to add from the point of view of the government, I would appreciate knowing it. While he is on his feet perhaps he could designate Tuesday, June 20, and Thursday, June 22, as allotted days, in accordance with the discussions I had with his colleague.

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, to answer the second question first, I am pleased to confirm that we will designate Tuesday and Thursday of next week as allotted days, the two remaining days in this period. As the opposition House leader realizes, today is an opposition day. Tomorrow and on Monday we will carry on with Bill C-56, if the debate continues until then. Then we will set aside the two opposition days which I have noted, and continue with the balance of Bill C-56 until it is concluded through third reading. Following that, we will call Bill C-36 and deal with report stage of the Export Development Act, then the language of trial bill at report stage, Bill C-42; next, the continuation of report stage of Bill C-48, the Customs Tariff Act, and on to Bill C-59, second reading of the bill affecting small businesses.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister's colleague indicated there might be some flexibility in the order of calling these bills. I wonder if the deputy House leader could indicate if that stands, and then we could discuss the order.
There has been a considerable amount of concern in the House about the case of Alexander Peter Treu. There has been some suggestion by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), supported by the hon. member for Windsor-Walker-ville (Mr. MacGuigan), that it might be appropriate for the House to consider establishing a special joint committee with the other place to deal with the Official Secrets Act. that kind of feeling on both sides of the House that it is perhaps time to examine that statute, would the deputy House leader convey this to his colleague and see if there can be some discussion about establishing a committee so that the matter could be examined in a way other than that which it has been heretofore?

subsubtopic: WEEKLY STATEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the first point, the government is always prepared to be flexible about the priorization, although we are committed to those particular bills. Our House leader will discuss that with House leaders of the respective parties.
With regard to a special committee to deal with the Treu case or the Official Secrets Act, I can indicate in a preliminary way that there is no disposition toward this at the present.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my comment will be brief. On June 8 the hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) raised by way of privilege the question of my misleading the House in my statement on "Measures to Strengthen and Encourage Research and Development in Canada", which I made to the House on June 1.
The hon. member made reference to two points in his remarks, and I would like to reply to both points, first on the question of gross national product versus gross domestic product.
Economists calculate gross domestic product on at least two different bases. No doubt it is this fact which has led the hon. member for Calgary Centre to suggest that a research and development expenditure target of 1.5 per cent of gross domestic product is substantially lower than a target of 1.5 per cent of gross national product.
In Canada gross domestic product is published at factor cost, but for international comparisons of R and D expenditures the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development calculate on what they term purchasers' values. The OECD calculation is higher because it includes indirect taxes less subsidies.
Point of Order-Mr. D. Munro
Based on this OECD definition of gross domestic product, which we have used for standard international comparisons, our target of 1.5 per cent of gross domestic product for 1983 translates to 1.46 per cent of gross national product. For practical purposes we believe in setting a five-year target; 1.5 per cent of gross domestic product, as I have used, is equivalent to a target of 1.5 per cent of gross national product, which is a much more widely known term.
The second point which the hon. member for Calgary Centre raised related to the question of accuracy of footnoting which appeared in the discussion paper. On that point, Mr. Speaker, the historical figures of Canadian research and development expenditures expressed in terms of gross national product which I used in my statement are the latest and most reliable data available from Statistics Canada and the cited "Bank of Canada Review." The research and development expenditures appear in a 1978 Statistics Canada publication on "Research and Development Expenditures in Canada, 1963-1977" and will in due course appear as revisions to the Statistics Canada Catalogue 13-003. Due to an oversight, the footnote to the table in my statement was not amended when the original data, from an August, 1977 publication, were changed to reflect the latest information available.
