subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
That a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons be appointed to consider and report upon the provisions of the Indian Act;
That fifteen members, to be named at a later date, act as members on the part of this House on the said committee;
That the said committee have the power to send for persons, papers and records and to examine witnesses; to sit during sittings and adjournments of the House; to report from time to time; to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be deemed advisable; and to delegate to sub-committees all or any of its powers except the power to report directly to the House;

June 15, 1978
Indian Affairs
That the committee have power to travel from place to place within Canada; and
That a message be sent to the Senate requesting that House to unite with this House for the above purpose, and to select, if the Senate deems it advisable, some of its members to act on the proposed Special Joint Committee.
He said; Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to say to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner), and to the government that the motion before the House is not viewed by my party as one of non-confidence.
The motion is in response to the serious problems afflicting the aboriginal people in Canada and holds the promise for a more enlightened Indian policy. One of the remarkable paradoxes in Canadian history is that at the very time Canadians are debating the historic constitutional rights of the two "founding races" we continue to proceed with a policy of assimilation of our aboriginal people.
There is irrefutable evidence that the policy of assimilation, which has been part of our political history, most recently expressed in a formal way in the policy white paper of 1969, has not only been rejected by the Indian community but more important has failed to resolve their serious social, economic, and political problems.
It is essential to have a brief glimpse of the past if we are to understand the present and forge a new future.
There has been considerable legislation affecting the Indians in Canada since the eighteenth century to the present. During this period, government policy has shown little variation from its original position of assimilation for Indian people into white society at the earliest possible time.
Prior to 1844 Indians were administered by the British Indian department, which was a branch of the military. Indian policy began when the government sought military alliances with the Indians to aid in war ventures, and to secure their friendship during peace time. After 1844 the administration of Indian Affairs was transferred to the Province of Canada, away from the authority in England.
By 1867 the Province of Canada had an intensely developed Indian policy administered by the Crown Lands Department. Two statutes passed in 1856, "An Act for the Better Protection of the Lands and Property of Indians in Lower Canada", and a similar act in Upper Canada, were introduced by government to protect the Indians and their lands from abuse only until such time as they became "civilized or assimilated".
In 1857 the Civilization of Indian Tribes Act expressly made assimilation its goal. It was declared that Indians who were "sufficiently advanced education wise or capable of managing their own affairs" would be enfranchised.
The Management of Indian Lands and Property Act declared the commissioner of the Crown lands to be the chief superintendent of Indian Affairs. He was vested with the power to dispose of lands reserved for the Indians which they had released or surrendered.
At confederation, the policy of the Province of Canada was inherited by the federal government in the British North

America Act, section 91(24), giving the government legislative authority over "Indians and lands reserved for Indians".
The bases of the policy were several: alienation of Indian interest in land through treaties; reservation of land for Indians; and the existence of a government department charged with managing the affairs of Indians. The main objective of the policy was to bring about a "detribilization" from the native way of life to that of the white majority. In 1868 the federal government integrated this policy into legislation which eventually became the basis of the first federal statute, the Indian Act of 1880.
The main quality running throughout this act was the pervading power of the superintendent general. The Indian Act of 1880 was not a new policy but rather an aggregation of previous legislation. The protectionist and assimilation attitudes of pre-confederation remained the central theme of the policy. This was apparent during Sir John A. Macdonald's speech during debate on second reading of the bill when he stated, as reported at page 1991, volume II, 1880, of the House of Commons debates:
We are bound to protect them-the general rule is that you cannot make the Indian a white man-all we can hope for is to wean them by slow degrees from the nomadic habits, which have almost become an instinct, and by slow degrees absorb them or settle them into lands. In the meantime, they must be fairly protected.
Despite subsequent revisions and modifications the 1880 Indian Act is in essence still in effect today, indicating that the Indian Affairs branch has undergone no major ideological shifts.
During the years 1946 through 1948 a joint special committee of the Senate and House of Commons considered the Indian Act and the general administration of Indian Affairs. The 1946 hearings dealt mainly with witnesses from the Indian Affairs Department. The thrust of their argument, that more funds and a larger and more highly paid staff would solve the problems, failed.
The hearings represented the first attempt to consult the Indians themselves on such matters as treaty rights, the Indian Act, enfranchisement and band membership. However, only two major briefs were submitted by Indian associations. The presentation by Dr. Diamond Jenness, an anthropologist, entitled "The Liquidation of Canada's Indian Problem within Twenty-five Years", was widely heralded, and with the exemption of abolishing reserves and enfranchisement, the plan was substantially implemented.
These proposals formed the backbone of Indian Affairs philosophy and was reflected in the 1969 white paper, the 1975 local government guidelines, and the James Bay legislation.
As a result, the present Indian Act was passed in parliament in 1951 which primarily consolidated all previously independent changes. Although in some minor ways the 1951 act was a slight improvement, there was little change in the federal government's restrictive attitudes toward Indian rights and freedoms.
The 1959 joint committee was not established to study a revision of the Indian Act, but devoted its energies and gather-
June 15, 1978

ing of material to issues such as education, housing and band funding, which eventually lead to some amendments.
In the intervening periods, a commendable study on education was carried out under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson). Otherwise, virtually nothing occurred until the June, 1969, white paper. The white paper introduced by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) proposed the abolition of the Indians' special constitutional position, repeal of the Indian Act, and phasing out of the Department of Indian Affairs. In total it denied the existence of an Indian cultural and political reality.
At the time of the tabling of the white paper, my colleague, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), stated on June 25, 1969, as reported at page 10583 of Hansard:
It would be callous gamesmanship and a very real tragedy if this statement had any other inspiration than a genuine attempt to help the Indian people.
The white paper was rejected by the Indian community and the Indian sentiments were expressed in the red paper of 1970, prepared by the Indian chiefs of Alberta, who described the 1969 policy as:
A scheme whereby a generation or shortly after the proposed Indian Lands Act expires, our people would be left with no land; and consequently the future generation would be condemned to the despair and ugly spectre of urban poverty in ghettos.
They recommended that the Indian Act should be reviewed by Indian people but should not be repealed. The paper went on to say:
The only way to maintain our culture is for us to remain as Indians. To preserve our culture it is necessary to preserve our status, rights, lands and treaties. Our treaties are the basis of our rights.
The review process of the Indian Act commenced in the Indian community, and that process continues and will be invaluable in the revision of the act. In response to the obvious fact that the Indian view was essential when determining how the Indian Act would be changed, a joint cabinet and National Indian Brotherhood committee was established to determine the best way to amend the Indian Act to suit the future needs of Indians. After lengthy discussions between the committee of the National Indian Brotherhood and representatives of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of Justice, an Indian Act consultative process was agreed upon by the joint National Indian Brotherhood cabinet committee on December 12, 1975. To date that process has met with failure. I have no doubt the minister's comments of last Friday in response to the NIB withdrawal from the joint cabinet committee will be used by the minister in an effort to convince the House that progress has been made and that the situation is well in hand. That tactic will not succeed.
The joint National Indian Brotherhood cabinet committee has undoubtedly served a useful function and may do so in the future. However, I am not convinced it is the most appropriate structure to deal effectively with the Indian Act. Let us have no illusions as to who will shoulder the blame and suffer the
Indian Affairs
consequences if the joint committee fails in its objectives; it will be the Indian leaders and the Indian people, not ministers of the Crown.
Why do I have reservations about the existing structure? The government, despite the withdrawal of its policy white paper, has through administrative and legislative action continued to pursue a policy of assimilation and integration. The 1975 local government guidelines which we debated in this chamber on June 12, 1975, were based on the principle of assimilation. The James Bay legislation, by setting a precedent under which the Cree and Inuit decided to accept lands under provincial jurisdiction, is a glaring example of the assimilation policy pursued by the present government. Under these circumstances I ask: are this government and its ministers to be trusted with an issue as fundamental as the Indian Act?
The joint NIB cabinet committee, by its very nature, is shrouded in secrecy, and this prevents members of parliament, the Indian community, and the public from assessing the motives and actions of the government. During the past decade, matters before cabinet have been hidden from the public under the guise of cabinet secrecy. Lack of information constantly thwarts our attempts to ensure responsible, open administration, and the government has not been timid in exploiting every opportunity for political gain. Such a committee is advantageous to the cabinet, but a liability to the Indian leaders, the Indian community, and to parliament.
We should recall that by introducing the white paper in 1969 the government skillfully trapped Indian organizations into supporting the Department of Indian Affairs. The government knew the white paper would be rejected by the Indian community and that it would be forced to accept the only alternative available at the time-support for a department committed to assimilation and integration. We all know the Department of Indian Affairs has increased in size since this manoeuvre was carried out, and has extended its influence over the Indian people. Again, the question should be asked: is this the most appropriate structure, knowing the department plays an integral part in the negotiation process and recognizing that it is ingrained with the philosophy of paternalism and assimilation?
The current situation in Canada is not unlike that which existed in the United States in 1969 At that time the findings of a government study commissioned by President Nixon stated that the termination issue in the United States still "poisons Indian affairs and causes almost every act of government to be viewed with suspicion."
The government has antagonized Indian leaders in all areas of the country, producing a polarizing effect on the policy of assimilation. Many Indians see assimilation and integration written into every administrative decision and, as a result, are frequently reluctant to accept help. At times they refuse help which is desperately needed because they fear and believe that to do so would lead to a further undermining of their rights. The policy of assimilation has had dire consequences for the Indian people both in political and human terms.

June 15, 1978
Indian Affairs
Important issues such as Indian culture and identity, consultation and self-determination, rights and treaties, hunting and fishing rights, education, health, economic viability of reserves, urban migration, enfranchisement and membership, are but a few of the political problems which remain unsolved.
Last Friday the minister made reference to the enfranchisement of Indian women. The hon. gentleman knows members of all political parties have expressed their concern about the matter and are anxious to see the Indian Act revised. However, if the minister was serious in his statement-and I have no reason to doubt his sincerity-then he must realize it is essential to review the broader question of enfranchisement and membership. The minister knows the law not only affects Indian women but discriminates against Indian men and Indian children. My colleagues will enlarge on a number of these issues as the debate progresses.
In human terms, present conditions are scandalous. An infant mortality rate of 40 per 1,000 live births among the Indian community compares with 21 per 1,000 live births among Canadians generally. A suicide rate of 20 per 100,000 population compares with a national figure of 9.7 per cent; 87 per cent of Indians live in sub-standard housing as compared to 11 per cent for the rest of Canadians; 54 per cent of Indian households receive incomes of under $2,263 per annum, while the figure for other Canadians receiving similar incomes is 20 per cent. The life expectancy for Indian people is 36 years as compared with 62 years for the rest of the population. Only 6 per cent of Indians complete high school education though the figure throughout Canada is 88 per cent.
It is now apparent that the serious social, economic, and political problems experienced by the Indian community will not be resolved until we can assure the Indian people that it is our desire and intention to honour the special relationship between the federal government and themselves. Such an assurance could best be achieved by bringing in a new Indian Act which derives its authority from the British North America Act. Such an act should be a sensitive and accurate reflection of the views of the Indian community.
The Indian Act is the single most important piece of legislation affecting Indian people. By its very nature it focusses on virtually all the fundamental issues relating to Canada's Indians, including their continued existence as an identifiable culture.
The issue involves minority rights, acquired rights, and aboriginal rights. Since the past has too often seen misunderstanding and misinterpretation of Indian rights and liabilities, it is essential that the Indian people be active participants in the deliberations. In our search for solutions in the past we have either intentionally or unintentionally attempted to impose our values on a minority group. It is therefore not surprising that the Indian people may well reject many of our values. This should not be viewed as a failure of our system, nor as individuals should our personal values be perceived as being inadequate or threatened. Rather, we should view the differences as the expression of a people attempting to retain its culture and identity. It is therefore essential that members

of the House of Commons and of the other place-and, indeed, all Canadians-have a clearer understanding of these differences.
Those with a knowledge of the Indian Act and related matters are aware of the voluminous legal opinions which have accumulated over the years. I have no doubt that such documents will be of immeasurable assistance to those involved in the deliberations. However, since we are dealing with a disadvantaged minority, it would be useful to remind hon. members of an observation which is frequently made in discussions concerning equality, and specifically legal equality, as it relates to a disadvantaged group. Individuals who have equality in fact or who have a very strong bargaining position usually find legal equality invaluable. For those in a position of political and economic weakness, legal equality alone serves the stronger interest in society at the expense of the weak.
To a group struggling to assert and protect a special identity, equality may in fact be a negative concept. I am confident that such a committee would recognize this fact, and its discussions would be based not only on legal evidence but also on the basis of the human elements involved in the issue.
1 want to make one additional comment on why it is necessary to review the Indian Act and the reason for proposing a joint committee of both Houses to assist in the task. To me, an additional compelling reason for this motion is to ensure that the aboriginal people of Canada have a meaningful input into the national unity debate. The government document "A Time for Action" tabled in the House of Commons on June 12, 1978, is long on rhetoric but short on substance. It does not suppress the fears that the concepts forming the basis of the white paper of 1969 have been put to rest.
When the white paper was introduced in 1969 by the present Minister of Finance two legal concepts were used to support the policy of the government, and I think we should be reminded of these. The first concept was that the legal basis for special Indian claims is untenable, that treaties should be terminated, and that aboriginal claims are not real claims. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was forced to reverse his position, and considerable research and a growing body of information regarding this issue have accumulated rapidly in the last few years. However, 1 notice that no reference is made respecting this important matter in the document which was tabled by the Prime Minister.
Second, it was asserted that the division of powers in the British North America Act which makes Indians a federal responsibility is discriminatory and leads to inferior services. It was reasoned that the separate legal status of Indians is charged with keeping the Indian people:
-apart from and behind other Canadians. The Indian people have not been full citizens of the communities and provinces in which they live.
Thus, in 1969 the conclusion was that Indians should become wards of the provinces. Although the argument of the government was and continues to be unfounded, we have seen
June 15, 1978

the James Bay legislation which confirms that the original concept of the government is still being pursued.
We also know that provincial governments have and continue to include Indian people in provincial programs. In addition, the federal government has not been reluctant or timid to use its strong fiscal arm either to entice or to coerce provinces into cost-shared programs, with the expressed intention of assisting regional disparity and helping the disadvantaged.
The argument of the government for transferring responsibility for Indians to the provinces is, therefore, specious. The critical issue, I must repeat, is the federal financial responsibility and constitutional responsibility, and surely the timing is appropriate for a joint committee of both Elouses to study this specific issue.
Following the rejection of the policy in the white paper, research and negotiations over aboriginal rights and treaty rights have intensified, as I indicated earlier. In addition, the National Indian Brotherhood, provincial organizations, and bands have been actively reviewing and consolidating their position with respect to revisions to the Indian Act.
I recognize that the issues are complex and that difficult questions remain to be answered, but I must conclude that the Indian people and their leaders are now better prepared to make a substantive and constructive contribution to a joint committee than at any time in their history. I have no doubt that the Indian leaders across Canada are genuinely concerned about whether they have the political cohesiveness necessary to undertake such a project. That feeling is understandable, and in many ways is analogous to the feelings of Canadians who are reflecting on the broader question of national unity.
If the Indian community desires a more definitive role in confederation, and I have no doubt that that is its view, it must avoid the hazard of being engulfed and forgotten in the broader debate. The responsibilities are onerous, and the path will be difficult. Each of us, whether we are Indian or nonIndian, can be immobilized by the threat of failure. The risk is not failure but, rather, the possibility that the voice of Canada's aboriginal people will be but a whisper or unheard as events pass before us. Such a joint committee would be invaluable as a repository for such a dialogue at this critical time in our history.
In conclusion, let me summarize by stating that the motion was introduced in the knowledge that existing conditions affecting Indian people are unacceptable in both economic and human terms, in the knowledge that meaningful progress in resolving major issues will be impossible until the Indian people are reassured about their rights and relationship with the federal government, and with the conviction that a thorough study of the Indian Act by a joint parliamentary committee, whose mandate and terms of reference are acceptable to the Indian people, will provide the basis for a responsible, sensitive report which will not only allay the present fears of the Indian people but also offer them hope for the future.
A nation's image and the character of its people is reflected in their attitudes toward the disadvantaged. This motion would
Indian Affairs
provide Canada and Canadians with an opportunity to recognize the important contribution the aboriginal people have made to our nation, and would give us a chance to recognize the importance of their culture and indentity, and to ensure that justice will be served.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague, the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth), who is usually the spokesman for our party on questions such as this, is in his constituency, and he has asked me to speak on behalf of our party and to express some of the views he has on the motion before us today and on the whole question of the problems of native people in this country.
Let me begin by saying that we will support the motion put forward by the official opposition although, since we believe in the abolition of the Senate, we can hardly be said to be enthusiastic about the part of the motion which would provide for membership on the proposed committee of members of the Senate.
However, the problems of native people in this country, both status and non-status, are so tremendous, and native people are in such a perilous situation-they are obviously at the bottom of the ladder in every facet of life in this country which is of importance to the people-that we welcome this opportunity to discuss their problems today, and we are prepared to support the appointment of a committee such as the one proposed by the official opposition.
Hon. members should give some thought to the actual situation. According to the 1971 census there were 295,000 native Indian people in Canada. The average income of Indians on reserves for the last year for which we have figures, 1974-75, was $1,959. The national average income for the same year was $8,200. In other words, the national average was more than four times as great as the average income of native people living on reserves. Do I need to remind members of the House of how poorly any family can live when the average income of a person is less than $2,000 a year? Most of them live in isolated areas in which the cost of many basic essentials of living is much greater than it is in the settled parts of Canada.
There is another problem. Any member of parliament who represents an area with a growing native population-and I represent a part of Winnipeg which has seen an explosion of the native population in recent years-knows that when they are moving into the city, native people are at the lowest economic level of any of the people in the area. Let us look at some facets of native existence. In our federal prisons, of the 9,100 persons held in those prisons, 568 were Indian, 180 were Metis and 115 were Inuit. Since native people make up only 2 per cent of Canada's population, it is obvious that our native people are greatly overrepresented in our prisons, probably ten times as much as they should be.
If one looks at the provincial jails, the percentage of native inmates, especially in western Canada, is staggering. In the

June 15, 1978
Indian Affairs
case of one institution for women that I know, the percentage runs to over 90 per cent of the total inmate population.
Let us look at infant mortality rates. A couple of years ago the infant mortality rate in Canada as a whole was 15 deaths per 1,000 births; for Indian people it was 38.6 deaths per 1,000 births, and for Inuit it was 53.2 deaths per 1,000 births. When one looks at education, the minister can say that we have made great strides, that native children are staying in schools longer than they had in earlier years. What is happening at present is that native children get to grade 10, but in grade 10 there is a mass exodus. We are not succeeding in holding native children in the high schools more than a fraction of what we do for children who attend Canadian high schools as a whole. Given this situation, I say that we have a crisis.
I was disappointed that the resolution put forward today simply proposed the setting up of a committee to study the Indian Act. It seems to us that simply to study the act would be a mistake, that the problems of the native people are much greater and go much further than simply what is incorporated in the act.
If we are going to discuss the act, there is one provision of the act with which we need to deal because there has been so much discussion amongst the native people themselves. It is an issue which was raised by the hon. member who introduced this debate, and that is the section in the Indian Act which discriminates against native women as against the men. The situation is really quite simple. There is no question that Indian women have been treated unfairly and unjustly, and there is no question that justice must be done, that Indian women's equal rights with Indian men must not only be recognized but restored. The Indian women who are unjustly treated must receive restitution and compensation.
We believe that this unjust and discriminatory section of the Indian Act was brought in, not by Indians but by white political leaders and by white bureaucrats who probably wanted to make their work easier, and to reduce the number of status Indians. We think that that situation cannot and should not continue, and we think it should be rectified by simply striking out the section in the current Indian Act which creates that discriminatory situation, and inserting a clause retroactively reinstating those women and their children who have suffered from that section. I say to the minister that if the government is prepared to bring forward that kind of amendment, he will get agreement from this party to pass it with very little, if any, debate, and I think the same would be true of the other parties. If the minister really believes that this should be done, he should proceed with it and not plead lack of time for debate.
I am concerned about what this year's estimates show in the way in which the government is curtailing expenditures for services for the native people. The estimates for 1978-79 call for an expenditure of $650 million. That is an increase of just $17 million over last year's estimates. That works out, as far as I can calculate it, to an increase of less than 3 per cent. Surely the minister and the government recognize the fact that the cost of living is rising by something between 8.5 per cent and

10 per cent at present. Surely they recognize that just to hold the services where they were last year, an increase of 8.5 per cent to 10 per cent is required. Yet what we see is that the increase proposed, and therefore the increase for the department, is less than 3 per cent. I think this makes that kind of proposal for dealing with the problem of the poorest people in this country a national disgrace. Native people have often wondered whether the department and its personnel are employed to help native people meet their needs, or whether they are employed simply to give well paid, comfortable employment to several thousand white people.
Let me indicate briefly what I mean, in the figures which I have been able to accumulate. 1 will use some figures supplied by the government in response to questions I put on the order paper about 18 months ago which were answered on March 21, 1977. In 1975-76 the department employed 11,543 people; in Ottawa it employed 2,375 people. According to the figures the government provided-and I think I added them correctly, but if they are wrong, they will not be wrong by very much- the number of native people employed by the department in Ottawa, out of 2,375 people two years ago, was just 59. In the 1978-79 estimates we see that the manpower in Indian and Eskimo affairs programs will be 5,913. Of these, three are 26 executives, 2,000 in scientific and professional fields, 1,390 in the administrative and foreign service, 194 in the technical fields, 1,010 in the administrative support section, and 1,289 in the operational section. How many of the people who receive incomes of $25,000 or more are native people? I do not have the figures, but the minister and I know that the percentage would be no more than one or two.
I should like to refer to a press release dated March 8, 1977. It was issued by the Public Service of Canada. The subject is: "Native Employment in the Pubic Service is Studied". Mr. Gallant, the Chairman of the Public Service Commission, said the following:
Native people comprise about 4 per cent of the Canadian population, but they occupy less than 0.5 per cent of the officer-level positions in the public service.
It would be surprising if native people felt that white people were doing well when supposedly dealing with aboriginal misery. How much of the budget is used for the benefit of natives? Mr. Gallant has indicated that the government has done poorly in the field of employment for native people, even within the department which supposedly deals with Indian and Eskimo problems.
Dealing with the area of grants and contributions, last year $2.8 million was provided for research into Indian treaties and rights. This year only $2.2 million will be provided, which is a reduction of $600,000. Have the problems concerning Indian treaties and aboriginal rights been solved? Has an agreement been reached? Of course not. Are the differences between the government and native people becoming more apparent? Is the government putting pressure on native organizations by cutting back their funds? As far as I am concerned, that is the

June 15, 1978

real reason. Native organizations are entitled to an explanation of that cutback.
Dealing with the area of contributions under agreements with the provinces for the provision of welfare and other services, as well as contributions to Indian associations and groups, last year the contributions totalled $29 million. This year they have been reduced to $21 million, which is a decrease of $8 million. Why? Is there less need for welfare? Do the Indian bands and associations require less assistance with their problems? I do not believe that. If that money is not to be paid out in the form of welfare, perhaps it should be used for economic development. Approximately $24 million was provided for Indian and Eskimo economic development. That has been reduced to $22 million, which is a decrease of $2 million. Money for both welfare and economic development for native people has been cut back, at a time when needs are greater and costs are rising.
In the last 15 years the government has changed from an authoritarian and paternalistic approach to consultation and dialogue. It seems to be returning to the area of more big brother pressure. At one point larger amounts of money were provided for education and welfare, and then cutbacks occurred. There was the beginning of thinking in terms of employment for all native people, and then there was lack of action. At one point money was provided for economic development, and then cutbacks occurred.
What has been Ottawa's response to this crisis? When native people leave reserves and come to the cities, Ottawa takes the view that they become a problem of the cities and provinces. In cities such as Winnipeg, Regina and Calgary, just to mention a few, native people constitute a high proportion of the welfare cases, child neglect cases, the jail population, and the alcoholism problem. When native people remain on the reserves they are the responsibility of the federal government. Once they move into the cities, Ottawa indicates that they are no longer a federal government responsibility and washes its hands of them. The headaches and the problems are left to the cities and provinces. The situations and the problems of native people are the responsibility of all people in this country and on this continent. The native people of this continent have been mistreated since the day white men arrived.
A solution to native problems will not be reached easily. It will take more money than we are willing to spend. It will require more consultation and co-operation with native organizations than we have been willing to partake in. If we are willing to work with the native people, a solution to the problem which has bedevilled this continent for more than 200 years will be reached. If those approaches are taken, we can look forward to the day when native people will live in socioeconomic conditions equal to the rest of Canada. That has not been reached yet, and I see no real desire on the part of the government to attain that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion we are debating calls for the appointment of a Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons to consider and report upon the provisions of the Indian Act. I was somewhat surprised by this motion because the House of Commons already has the Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development whose members may, if they so desire, obtain the permission of Parliament to carry out special studies dealing with Indian affairs.
That committee can also be empowered to call witnesses and travel. That has been done in the past. I myself was once a member of such a committee; we met with Indians and Inuit in their communities, and we were able then to hear their comments and recommendations on Indian affairs. The only thing that can be added to that committee is the presence of senators to make the same studies which were made before. I say the same studies but it will certainly not be the same studies because although the same problems exist in certain areas, that committee will certainly have fresh recommendations to make.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that with respect to Indian affairs some things are wrong in Canada. In his speech the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) mentioned his fears of seeing Indians being assimilated to our way of life. I believe he may be a bit right and the danger that exists of seeing that assimilation occur might perhaps be confirmed when we see particularly large projects being carried out such as one currently in progress in the province of Quebec with respect to the James Bay power development project. We have one slated to start soon in the Yukon Territory,namely the pipeline to be built across Alaska, the Yukon and part of Alberta to the United States. There is another one planned from the King Christian Islands and Ellesmere Islands for the transportation of natural gas to eastern Canada and the United States. Those are large projects bringing with them in those regions large numbers of white men with modern methods, modern techniques and, in short, all their ways of life.
Today you only have to consider what is happening on the James Bay work sites and you can see that workers expect more than they did in the past. Today they want to have as much comfort as possible and I believe that is reasonable too. They want as much comfort as possible to do that work. Indians working on those projects are inclined to follow our working methods, to take our lifestyle and I am not sure yet that that is good for them because they do not seem to be prepared to accept or learn fast enough that transition from one life style to another.
So when we discussed the pipeline project on August 4, 1977, in the speech that I made on that occasion I pointed out to the government that I agreed in principle with the project proposed by Foothills Pipe Lines (Yukon) Ltd. but I had

June 15, 1978
Indian Affairs
reservations and I would like to name a few here having regard precisely to the Indians in that region, and I quote:
That the government negotiate with our native people, with every consideration they are entitled to as original owners of the territories concerned.
This is a reservation which I was making on the occasion of the debate on the pipeline. I added:
That it allow them to assert themselves without imposing upon them a way of life to which they were not born and, as our needs for natural gas are very relative, without imposing any temporal constraints upon them as has been the case with the James Bay Inuit with regard to negotiations.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, I suggest once again that in all projects of this magnitude one must be very careful and this is where I think that the fears which the member for Lambton-Kent alluded to are justified. In our past relations with the Indians, I think we do not have much to brag about when it comes to what we have given them, either in terms of the projects such as the one I just mentioned, and there have been others before, or in terms of exploration projects for tapping natural or other resources. What we have succeeded in giving them is alcoholism, tuberculosis and many other contemporary diseases caused by the weakening of their natural resistance to the elements.
Mr. Speaker, if this committee is struck, I think it will have to get some feed back from the Indians, and I should perhaps use the word Inuit. It will have to try and understand what they really want and what they expect from a government such as that of Canada. I think they want to participate in the development of this country as well in its economic activities, they want to participate in that in their own way and not in our way. This is what we, the white people, find difficult to understand. I think we must keep in mind quite clearly that they have their own way of living and that we should not proceed too quickly in trying to assuage them to our own way of life. I think this is where we are mistaken when we try to proceed too quickly.
Since Canada became a nation in early 1763, Indian affairs were administered by the British Crown. Starting in 1763, these responsibilities were transferred to the Canadian Crown. In 1912, with regard to the province of Quebec, there was the Quebec Boundaries Extension Act, but it was only towards the mid-60s that the Quebec government started to show some interest in Quebec Indian affairs. One cannot overlook the few errors made by the government at that time in dealing with the Indians or their affairs. Those errors were repeated by the present government to the extent where the Indians came to the federal government who accepted to provide them with an amount of about $10 million to help them defend themselves against the encroachments the provincial government was then planning by denying them almost all the rights they had to the lands entrusted to them by the act of 1912.
I think that, all in all, things worked themselves out not too badly, but mostly because the Indians had access to our courts and members of the judiciary who defended them and

obtained rulings that were favourable rather than unfavourable to them. So, I think those will be the tasks the committee will be entrusted with if it is created and, as far as I am concerned, it would be reasonable enough since such a committee has not gone out to the northern communities for several years now.
True, Justice Berger's Commission went around the main Indian communities affected by the development of the pipeline, but many other Indian localities and regions have not been visited for a very long time, and I think that the committee could gather some interesting and important information for the government and the minister. It could also change the government's policy by recommending measures that would be more satisfactory for the Indians. I think we should accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Lambton-Kent to reshape that committee, not to reshape it but to add to it members from the Senate, to make it a joint committee and to allow it to meet Indians from all parts of Canada, hear their opinions and make the changes that are necessary to meet their demands.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to start off by expressing disappointment with the approach to the resolution. I have no doubt that the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), in his characteristic and bipartisan way, has attempted to put forward a useful proposal to deal with a difficult issue that has remained unresolved for a period of years despite a great deal of effort by governments, parliamentary committees, and Indian associations in attempting to come to grips with it.
My disappointment, I suppose, stems from the rather lengthy and over-laboured treatment of an issue which is at least ten years old, namely the 1969 policy paper. I would remind the hon. member for Lambton-Kent that it is now 1978. I think there have been at least three ministers who have disavowed the direction of that paper. I know that my predecessor, who is here in the House today because of the debate, others before him, and also myself, have repeated with all the conviction and eloquence that we can severally muster, that we are not talking about assimilation. That is not our purpose; that is not our objective; it is quite different from that.
Despite all those assertions and the concrete steps taken by the government to move to support Indian self determination, the key spokesman for the official opposition, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, on an occasion when he could have addressed the difficulties with the Indian Act, spent most of his time going over history-quite interesting but not particularly germane-and then went into a protracted discussion of the 1969 white paper. I do not know if anyone on this side of the House-I am not sure about the other side-is any wiser
June 15, 1978

about precisely how the official opposition would deal with the Indian Act other than to send it to a standing committee.
If there is a subject that has been debated, studied, agonized over, worried about, disputed and contended-if it is not the constitution, then it is the Indian Act. Even the Indians are becoming a little impatient, I suspect, with our inability, often in conjunction with them, to deal with the basic constitutional background that governs their lives internally and their relationship with the Government of Canada, the Crown, and the people of Canada.
I know that the hon. member is trying to do this with immense good will. I must tell him that we will probably be voting against it, however, largely because we see it as a set-back. We are not at the point to refer this issue-which has been under discussion, under analysis, has been studied and had workshops for five or six years-holus-bolus to a joint committee and ask it to come up with an answer to problems with which we have made slow progress. I know the hon. member for Lambton-Kent will in part understand my disappointment and why the issue will not be dealt with that way.
I do not want to labour my disappointments today, because actually I am in a more positive mood than my remarks would indicate. I will come to that in a second, but as I must express some disappointment with the Conservative party, I must also say I was a little disappointed with the New Democratic Party. I have taken into account, however, that as the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) pointed out, he was pinch-hitting for the hon. member for the Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth). He rather skirted around the Indian Act and tended to treat it as a peripheral or marginal issue. I do not have much to disagree with him on some of the things he said regarding jobs, programs, education and other things, and I think the parliamentary secretary will deal with some of these matters when he speaks.
We tend to minimize the significance of dealing with the Indian Act. If there is an analogy it is the analogy of the urgency and importance we attach to dealing with the Canadian constitution.

There is a stage in these things where I am prepared to see a parliamentary committee work, but it is not now and I will come to what I hope to do instead. Hon. members may come around to seeing the wisdom of my proposal versus theirs. I do not want to be partisan because I would like to enter this discussion and debate in a healthy spirit of mutual respect and willingness to bring it to a head.
Let me repeat that the Indian Act is not a peripheral issue, it is not marginal, it is central. Unless we can deal with it with the best will in the world, governments or departments will not achieve the objectives that the Indians have today. What is central to amending the Indian Act is at long last to deal with the core issue, and that is the powers of the chiefs and the band counsels-at long last to deal with the powers vested in the minister, powers which today are anachronisms at best. It is only through amending the Indian Act that we can achieve
Indian Affairs
that transfer of responsibility from a minister and a government to the duly elected people, the bands, namely, the chiefs and the band counsels. That transfer of responsibility is the only way we will see the sort of development for which we hope.
I am committed to amending the Indian Act. The last major revision was in 1950. The act no longer reflects the needs or the interest of the Indian people, nor does it adequately reflect a proper role for the minister. When we begin to examine the process of amending the Indian Act there is one question we must be clear on and, if we are not, the NIB will be clear on it for us.
I should like to direct the attention of the House to the presence in the gallery of the NIB representatives, particularly its president, which reflects their interest in this debate.

speechtext:
Conversations with the president of the NIB, members of its executive or president of provincial associations or chiefs will serve to remind the House that any amending process cannot touch, eliminate, or affect the trust responsibilities of the minister, the historic links with the treaties and, in turn, the links between the treaties and the Crown. If we start meddling in that relationship I think we can forget about getting any sort of co-operation from the Indian people in the process of amending the Indian Act. Those links are not just symbolic. To the Indians I have met, they are real and symbolic. They are the principle, the legal, and constitutional connection. Any attempt to fiddle with that will compromise the whole exercise. We have to be clear that that issue, that part of it, is not open for discussion and negotiation.
We must also be clear that in the exercise we are engaged in, that what we are attempting to do on the one hand is to preserve those historic and important links with the past and on the other hand trying to frame a law which will provide new opportunities for the future. Those new opportunities essentially relate to band government, local powers, and things of that kind. I say that simply to reassure the House that I am anxious to amend the Indian Act. I have indicated that to the President of the National Indian Brotherhood and to other provincial association presidents. I am anxious not to lose time as a result of the interregnum caused by the breakdown of the NIB cabinet committee process. I am anxious to continue consultation, and I can tell the House today that continuing consultations are a reality between myself and the president of the NIB, as well as others, and among our staffs. I think there is a general disposition to deal with these issues.
Getting back to the motion, I doubt that one will find there is widespread support that we should simply refer it to a parliamentary committee. I would be anxious, and I hope the Indian leadership will support me on this, to continue to build on the work that has been done prior to the joint NIB cabinet committee during its hearings, and in the future.

To deal with the suggestion that not much has happened or that not much has been accomplished, in this connection I would like to review some of the areas of broad agreement that have emerged from the joint NIB-cabinet discussions to give the House some indication of the basis on which I would see the pulling together of the work done to date. I am surprised the hon. member for Lambton-Kent cjid not deal with it at greater length. When there are a lot of people in a room trying to get an agreement by definition, it is much more difficult than trying to get two people to come to an agreement There were considerable hurdles, suspicions-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
He would only have complicated it further by just one more voice, reasonable voice as it is. There were serious hurdles to overcome in making this process work. But despite all of that, there were some important developments. In the process, broad agreement has been reached on at least some of the following principles and objectives. The New Indian Act should be regarded by the government, by the parliament, and by Canadians generally as a special constituent law governing the whole relationship between the Indian people and government, and in effect with the larger society as a whole. It should contain a preamble or declaratory section attesting to the continued special status of Indians in Canada, to their aboriginal descent and historical link with the Crown, to the treaty rights for the need to preserve and protect their Indian laws, and to the on-going responsibility of the federal government.
An important point I think we agreed to, and one I am still sort of mulling over, concerned the fact that the revision should be phased rather than an attempt made at wholesale revision. For this reason some of the earlier revisions might subsequently require further modification as later revisions are made. My own feeling on this is that we should try to deal with as much as possible, and if we find that in the process of trying to amend the totality of the Act leads to no progress on some of the substantive areas of agreement, we should approach it in a phased way. I think that is generally agreed with the NIB as well.
There should be an elective or opting-in principle which would allow bands wishing to do so to take advantage of revised provisions of the act, particularly in the area of band

government. This elective principle is intended to take account of the fact that bands all across the country are at various stages of development, requiring flexibility in the legislation to respond to their particular needs.
This opting-in principle would be exercised through a clearly defined procedure for band referendum, which could also be the means whereby bands would make all their major decisions.
The underlying aim of the first phase of Indian Act revision, perhaps of most revisions would be-and this is absolutely crucial-to enlarge the powers, functions and responsibilities of bands to enable them to take charge of their own affairs in ways and means of their own choosing.
One area where we had some difficulty concerned the preamble section. What happened basically was that discussions about the philosophy of the act kept running up against difficult questions of how it might be expressed in its operative sections. One thing we had decided to do was deal with the preamble later in the process but still within the framework of the first phase of the revisions. Accordingly, in the past year or so discussions have tended to focus on a number of specific subjects of particular concern and interest to Indian bands in various parts of the country.
Top priority has been given, for example, to ways and means of giving effect to the agreed policies of Indian control of Indian education. Members of the House who were also members of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development a few years ago will recall how that policy evolved with substantial assistance and advice from the standing committee. Since that time an increasing number of bands have been able, through administrative arrangements, to assume local control of Indian education through the establishment of school boards and other means. What is desired by the Indian people, and what is indeed needed now, is a solid statutory base for the transfer or delegation of authority and responsibilities now exercised by the minister under the act, without diminishing his fundamental responsibility in relation to Indian education. How we define that will be an important area of discussion, and one I think we can resolve.
In the joint discussions so far there has been wide area of agreement on the practical measures for carrying out these transfers and delegations. But full agreement has foundered on differences in the NIB cabinet committee about the nature and extent of Indian rights in the field of education. That is still difficult. I recognize that, and it is something we will have to try to resolve.
In the matter of land surrenders, both the NIB and the government are agreed on the formula for allowing Indian bands to assume virtually full control of Indian lands for all purposes except outright sale. The Indians themselves have wished to preserve in the Indian Act the protection afforded to Indian lands by the surrender provisions relating to such sales.
As suggested, the central issues arising out of the current consideration of Indian Act revision relate to the future of band government. There seems to be wide agreement, for
June 15, 1978

example, that bands should be given the opportunity, or option, to acquire legal status and personality under the Indian Act, coupled with enlargement of band bylaw powers. It is recognized, however, that there are some difficult questions that need to be identified and resolved, for example, the extent, if any, that laws of general application, particularly provincial laws, would continue to be applied on reserves where the band government had assumed wide powers and responsibilities. That is an issue with which we will have to deal. There are also problems of bylaw enforcement and the administration of justice on Indian reserves generally.
As I suggested earlier, there is no disagreement with the need and desirability to enlarge band powers to allow those bands wishing to do so to take full control of their local affairs. In this regard we have been discussing a system of band charters, by which we mean negotiated agreements which would in effect become the constitution for the band concerned. The likelihood is that there would be some variation in these charters, in the form of categories of charter from which the bands could choose in order to meet their particular needs.
It is envisaged that the revised Indian Act could provide the statutory base for such a charter system, which would be open to bands wishing to exercise the option and expressing their wish through referendum. Other bands, and for some time this might include a majority of the 565 bands in the country today, might choose to remain under existing provisions of the Indian Act for the purposes of their local government. That would be a decision they would have to make. In other words, they would have a choice. That flexibility may be important in getting agreement to the Indian Act.
The intent in all this is to provide the flexibility of response which the government and Indian leaders agree is needed to meet the situation in which Indian bands today find themselves at various stages of political, social and economic development.
Finally, in these areas of current concern is the pressing question deriving from the discriminatory aspects in the present act in relation to Indian women. The government has decided that such discrimination is no longer tolerable in our society and we know that this view is broadly, if not unanimously, shared in both Houses of Parliament. Ministers have informed the Indian leaders, through the NIB cabinet committee, that the provisions discriminating against Indian women, and in particular section 12(l)(b), must be revised. While there is undoubtedly widespread and grave concern among the Indian bands about this complex issue of discrimination, I believe that there is growing awareness on the Indian side that it is an issue that must be resolved satisfactorily and as soon as possible. It is important to add that recently the NIB made a very significant statement in this regard. I think we are getting very much closer to an agreement about how this issue is to be dealt with.
I want to respond briefly to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) that somehow we treat this issue independent of a revision to the Indian Act. I
Indian Affairs
do not think that makes any sense at all. It would only exacerbate the feelings of the Indian people. It would appear to them that all the issues of basic importance to them are being put to one side while we preoccupy ourselves, admittedly with an important issue, one which we have agonized about a lot, and appear in this way to be insensitive to some areas of concern. Therefore I say it should be dealt with, but in the context of a range of amendments to the Indian Act.

I do not wish to conclude this statement without further reference to Indian rights as perceived by the Indian people. If one single issue can be said to have delayed or sidetracked proceedings in the NIB-cabinet committee and eventually led to the NIB's unilateral decision to withdraw from the committee, it was the broad and complex issue of Indian rights. Nor should we minimize that much work has to be done on these key questions to get them worked out in ways that would enable the federal government and provincial governments to give practical expression to the objectives which the Indian people are seeking in asserting such rights.
I believe that this work is continuing in a variety of ways and at different levels of contact with Indian groups. I have in mind in particular the tripartite arrangements that now exist in several provinces, involving senior representatives of the federal and provincial governments concerned and the leaders of provincial Indian associations. One way or another they are focusing on rights, issues and, particularly, on hunting and fishing rights, which I regard as crucial to the whole effort to reach a mutually satisfactory relationship between the Indian people and our wider society. I have asked my officials to give high priority to these admittedly difficult questions in interdepartmental consultations at the federal level, in claims negotiations, and in the tripartite working arrangements I just mentioned.
Hunting and fishing rights, and to some extent trapping and gathering rights as well, to my mind are central to the thinking of most Indians about their future identity in Canadian society. For people in the remote areas, it is a matter of lifestyle and even subsistence. For many other Indians it is a key element in continuing their culture. Without for a moment underestimating the complexities or the long, hard work that will be needed to bring about mutually satisfactory results, I am personally persuaded that we should include in our proposals for Indian Act revision, even in the first phase, some provision for safeguarding hunting and fishing rights which the Indian people maintain tenaciously are essential to their future well-being as Indians in this country.
What I have attempted to do is convey to the House that some substantial work has been done. Some areas for amendment have been identified. I hope I have conveyed to the House some sense of the direction we are moving in, the areas we would like to see amended in the first phase.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first reaction to the minister's remarks is of course, one of disappointment. The idea of establishing a joint House of Commons and Senate committee to study a variety of aspects relating to the hon. gentleman's portfolio is one which originated in the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs. It was advanced to the committee by the president of the National Indian Brotherhood. More important, it was one which was supported by the Liberal members of the committee.
Therefore we are disappointed that the minister should have chosen to advise and instruct the members of his party not to support what we consider to be a very important and fundamental exercise, especially in view of the debate which is going on today, a debate which is taking place in every corner of our country, by every level of government, by every segment of our society, and by all fair-minded and thinking people. I am talking, of course, about discussions on constitutional and institutional reforms to which all parties in this House are committed and which will affect all Canadians for all time to come. Of course, they will have very profound effects upon the native community as well.
The discussions include the protection of minority rights. As we read through the paper which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) tabled, we see that he views these rights of individuals and minority groups as being of fundamental concern to him. Again, Mr. Speaker, our native people are a highly visible minority group in our society, one which needs the trust, support, and help of us all. What about the rights of the Indians and Inuit? What about the contribution they made to the evolution and history of this country?
The debate today is timely because over the last ten years, since the introduction of the white paper in 1969, we have gained a much better understanding of Indian rights and the concerns and aspirations of the Indian community. A number of commissions and inquiries has been established and a number of authorities have given the government advice. One of those was the Indian Claims Commissioner who was appointed in 1969, Mr. Barber. There was Mr. Justice Berg-
Indian Affairs
er's study of the potential impact of massive industrial development in the Mackenzie Valley basin. Then there was the Lysyk inquiry in the Yukon, and the James Bay settlement, as well as the negotiations which have taken place in the Yukon with respect to the settlement-the extinguishment, as some people call it-of Indian claims in that region.
It was on the suggestion of the native groups which appeared before the committee that my hon. friend from Lambton-Kent introduced the motion we are debating today. I would reiterate that it was with the support of the Liberal members of that committee, and I am deeply disappointed that the minister should have taken his usual partisan stance by saying that his is the best proposal and that his alternative is the one that will be accepted by those he named, the National Indian Brotherhood. If they were so pleased with the way the government has reacted to their proposals in the past, they would still be on the joint NIB cabinet committee. They are not. The fact is that no concessions have been made by the government. All the things which were discussed were conditional on something-whether it was self-determination with respect to Indian education or whether it was an assumption of greater responsibility by bands and chiefs. There were conditions attached. The minister attached conditions to all the concessions which were being discussed.
There have been a number of previous inquiries of this kind, but I am saying that another one would be timely now because we are much better equipped. Native people have developed much better leadership over the last 25 years, and it would have to be the intention of the committee to include that leadership in a dialogue which might be carried out.
There were two previous inquiries of this kind. One was initiated in 1946. It sat through three sessions of parliament. When one reads through some of the transcripts, one can see that inquiry was brought about mainly because a number of native Indians had distinguished themselves during the Second World War and were returning home to find that their brothers in their home country were still being discriminated against, but in a manner much more offensive and oppressive than what they had seen abroad where they had been liberating people from oppressive authorities. The government consented to the appointment of an inquiry which was much like the one we are suggesting today. That inquiry sat through three sessions of parliament. It proposed some amendments to the Indian Act, which eventually became law in about 1950.
There was another special joint committee in 1961. That committee gave much thought to Indian self-government, but because of a change in government in 1963, no legislation resulted from those discussions.
I would like to refer to the basic concept of aboriginal rights and title, which is very important today because some aspects of special rights and privileges-the citizen plus status which our Indian and Inuit people have a right to demand-need to be enshrined in the Constitution. The Indian Act itself has not

June 15, 1978
Indian Affairs
been an effective enough tool to deal with this fundamental problem.
As my colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), has said, in order to identify and delineate the concept of aboriginal rights, one needs to go back over the history and evolution of the Indian Act. One needs to go back as far as the royal proclamation of 1763, which laid down the basic colonial policy which this government has followed. The policy was one of assimilation.
The policy was, as soon as possible and as quickly as feasible, to have Indians become Christians, and to enter into a period of transition which would take them from their traditional lifestyle, which was one of hunting, fishing, trapping and living with nature generally, to one of agriculture.
Even before that, in the early 1600s, white settlers in the maritimes and in the St. Lawrence Valley dealt with Indians in a different way than they did after the proclamation. They dealt with them as trading partners. They dealt with them in the fur trade, which was then the lifeblood of the economy of the North American continent.
In early history there was a different colonial policy, which was adhered to by the other partner, the other founding race. The maritime region was under French control. The King of France looked upon the native people as partners, not subjects. As a matter of fact, when in 1713 Acadia was ceded to the British Crown, it is contended by historians today that the King of France had no right to cede to the British Crown a sovereignty which he did not possess, namely, sovereignty over the native people in that area.
However, after 1763 the pattern was set. The proclamation formed the basis for the treaties which followed, but the treaties and the proclamation were never intended to be interpreted in the way they were. I wish to quote a short paragraph from a treaty which has been dealt with by courts, with regard to the question of aboriginal rights. Decisions have been made on this question. This treaty says:
And whereas it is just and reasonable and essential to our interests and the security of our colony that the several nations or tribes of Indians with whom we are connected and who live under our protection should not be molested or disturbed in the possession of such parts of our dominions and territories as, not having been ceded to or purchased by us are reserved to them or any of them as their hunting grounds-
The treaties which followed the proclamation were looked upon by Indian people as treaties of friendship and peace. They were not looked upon by the Indian people who signed them as a surrender of their traditional rights or as a sell-out of their land, which is more to a native person and his culture than it is to a white man. Our native friends tell us that the land is their soul and that the animals which live on the land are their spirits. One does not cede his soul, and one does not sell his spirit. The native people of this country have never done that.
Let me quote from an order in council setting up the treaty commission which studied and effected Treaty No. 8 in western Canada, as follows:

-that the Commissioner of the North West Mounted Police had pointed out the desirability of steps being taken for the making of a treaty with the Indians occupying the proposed line of route from Edmonton to Pelly River-
I am not going to go into the delineation of that area.
-Indians, were inclined to be turbulent and were liable to give trouble to isolated parties of miners or traders who might be regarded by the Indians as interfering with what they considered their vested rights-
So, Indians were turbulent, and there was a need for a peace treaty. That was what treaty No. 8, as with all other treaties, was all about.
This document states further, and I quote:
As it is in the interest of the Province of British Columbia, as well as in that of the Dominion, that the country to be treated for-
It does not say "ceded", but "treated for."
-should be thrown open to development and the lives and property of those who may enter therein safeguarded by the making of provision which will remove all hostile feeling from the minds of the Indians and lead them to peacefully acquiesce in the changing conditions-
From that we see that the treaty was intended to be a document of peace and friendship, but the final sentence of the quotation I just read says that the treaty was to be considered a tool for assimilating native people to our way of life. I repeat:
-and lead them to peacefully acquiesce in the changing conditions-
Indians were very skeptical about the men who came from afar to make these treaties. I quote from the commissioners' report on Treaty No. 8. It reads:
There was expressed at every point the fear that the making of the treaty would be followed by the curtailment of the hunting and fishing privileges... impressed with the notion that the treaty would lead to taxation and enforced military service. They seemed desirous of securing educational advantages for their children, but stipulated that in the matter of schools there should be no interference with their religious beliefs.
It is stated further:
Our chief difficulty was the apprehension that the hunting and fishing privileges were to be curtailed. The provision in the treaty under which ammunition and twine is to be furnished went far in the direction of quieting the fears of the Indians, for they admitted that it would be unreasonable to furnish the means of hunting and fishing if laws were to be enacted which would make hunting and fishing so restricted as to render it impossible to make a livelihood by such pursuits.
How naive the native people were in those days!
The report continues:
But over and above the provision, we had to solemnly assure them that only such laws as to hunting and fishing as were in the interests of the Indians and were found necessary in order to protect the fish and fur-bearing animals would be made, and that they would be as free to hunt and fish after the treaty as they would be if they never entered into it.
We assured them that the treaty would not lead to any forced interference with their mode of life, that it did not open the way to the imposition of any tax, and that there was no fear of enforced military service.
The natives had reason to be suspicious because Treaty No. 11 was almost a carbon copy of the treaties which were made in the south. Indians were to be converted to Christianity and to the pursuit of agriculture. It was for that reason that each Indian person was granted a tract of land of 160 acres per person, or 640 acres per family. One does not carry on
June 15, 1978

effective and life sustaining hunting and trapping on 640 acres. The intention was to convert natives to pursuing the same kind of life as the white society which had encroached upon them. The terms of the treaty demanded a peaceful acquiescence to the changing conditions. The process of assimilation did not work and Indians were very reluctant to agree to it. They were reluctant to be placed on reserves and to have that imposed on them.
This is an interesting document which I recommend to all my colleagues. It is one that accompanies this treaty, but it is not dissimilar from all the documents that have accompanied other treaties. It states here:
Indeed, the Indians were generally adverse to being placed on reserves. It would have been impossible to have made a treaty if we had not assured them that there was no intention of confining them to reserves. We had to very clearly explain to them that the provision for reserves and allotment of land were made for their protection, and to secure to them in perpetuity a fair portion of the land ceded, in the event of settlement advancing.
I do not know what was worse, confinement on the reserve or the granting of freedoms later on, such as the freedom to vote, which was granted to the natives in 1968, the freedom to buy alcohol in government stores, and the freedom to conform to the white man's way of life which ended in what some people call a slow process of annihilation and other people, who use a harsher term, call genocide.

Mr. Speaker, just before I speak on the motion I would like to refer to something that was said by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) at the beginning of his speech, if I understood him correctly. If I heard right, he said that the motion proposed today by the Conservative party was born in the standing committee where it received the support of all members. If that is what the hon. member said-and I am now having it checked out very carefully-then, to the best of my knowledge, he is not correct. What the committee agreed to do, if it completed its work on the estimates, was to have the annual report of the department referred to it so it could do more work in a general way as the steering committee decided. If the hon. member said what I thought he said, I plan to raise this at the first opportunity on a poinnt of order.
Now I wish to speak to the motion put forward today by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes). There is no doubt, as the minister himself said in his remarks, that this motion is well motivated and sincere. What the motion seeks to do is to establish yet another parliamentary committee to inquire into the problems facing the Indian people in Canada. It proposes to do so under the umbrella of the Indian Act in its present form, with all its imperfections and shortcomings, and all hon. members here know that there are many, many of those. The act in its present form is certainly unacceptable. Then it proposes that the committee would discuss the need for revisions of the Indian Act, and probably in time a report would issue from that committee on what the changes in the
Indian Affairs
act should be and how the act can be made more relevant in the view of the committee, more relevant to the modern day in which the Indian people in Canada are now living.
I respectfully submit that the hon. member, in attempting to have this motion approved by the House, is really turning back the clock. It is actually not a progressive step at all but a retrograde step. When I say that, it is not in any way to disparage the good intentions of my hon. friend opposite for I know him in his work in the committee to have a genuine concern and interest in the Indian people in Canada. He is truly one of the progressive members of his very conservative party.
