subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
Nor have I lost faith in the good work which can be done by parliamentary committees, given the right situation and acting at the appropriate time. Certainly, for example, it is the responsibility of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development to examine regularly and carefully the work of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to see that it is doing its job, as we expect it to, and that the public moneys which are used for programs to assist Indian people are put to the best use for the greatest benefit of Indian people.
Besides the examination of estimates and the clause by clause study of legislation, I believe also that parliamentary committees should be doing more investigative work. There should be frequent inquiries into national problems by committees of the House. But I argue that in this case, with respect to this proposal that a special joint committee be set up, the timing of the proposal of the hon. member is all wrong. It is much too late in the day for undertaking the establishment of the task force which is suggested by my hon. friend. In fact, to be blunt, it is something akin to a slap in the face to the Indian leaders in this country because it says in effect that all of the good, hard, productive, difficult work that they have done is of no account, that nothing has happened, and that a parliamentary joint committee should get down to work and do something because the Indian leaders have not done anything up to this point. I reject that suggestion and I say it is unfair, untrue, and a slap in the face to the Indian leaders of Canada.
The process of actual consultation with the Indian people and the task of reaching agreement on a revision of the Indian Act is already well under way, and the minister has gone into some detail to tell us about that. It has gone beyond the stage where a travelling joint committee could serve a very useful purpose.
While I do not wish to appear mean, nevertheless the motion today gives the impression that the Conservative party has just discovered that there is an Indian community in Canada. In this motion they say to the members of parliament that something must be done about Indian people and about the

June 15, 1978
Indian Affairs
outmoded Indian Act which has not been substantially revised for a long time. In fact, it has not been revised since 1951.
Hon. members opposite should know that a lot has happened already. In 1973 a proposed revision of the entire act emerged from a study done by an Indian group in Alberta. That study was funded by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. At the national level, a joint committee of the National Indian Brotherhood and the federal cabinet was established to deal with major policy issues arising as a result of the relationship between Indian people and the government. This committee had its first meeting in April, 1975, and there were subsequent meetings until April of this year when the NIB withdrew. Within that period of time a great deal of good, substantive work was done. The Brotherhood and Indian associations across the country remain determined to find a way to accomplish early and meaningful revisions of the Indian Act. Highly competent people are working within the National Indian Brotherhood. They are engaged in this difficult exercise, working along with the government through meetings to bring about revisions which will make this act relevant and make it do what Indian people expect.
The Government of Canada is more than prepared to meet, discuss, and find agreement for amendments. It may be done in phases so that the meetings, discussions, and agreements will have to take place again in the future. In the midst of all this solid, substantive, and valuable work, the Conservative party comes forward and indicates that we should strike a special joint committee, and send it out into the highways and byways of Canada. They speak about the need for a new Indian Act. It is similar to setting out to rediscover the wheel.
There have been special joint committees in the past. Hon. members opposite mentioned some of these. As well there have been ministerial inquiries. But the Indian people of Canada know that not much of value has come forth from all of this. There is a proposal in this motion to do again what was done before. We know there was little real progress in this difficult area until capable, dedicated Indian leaders applied themselves to this difficult task. Then we started to make progress. When the Indian Act is revised finally, it will be much more a tribute to those people than it will be to any of us in this place, or even in fact to the Government of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
I do not wish to be thought of as one who belittles in any way the roles of parliamentary committees, be they special, joint, or standing. There is much strength in our committee system. Most of the time it serves the people of Canada well. Of course there will be a time for a committee of this House to become deeply involved with revisions to the Indian Act. It may be after the bill, containing the revisions, has been given second reading in the House. Perhaps it will be earlier, as was suggested by the minister.
It may be necessary for the minister to take a federal position. That position will be dealt with by cabinet and then referred to the standing committee. I believe a great deal of good work could be done if that took place. There is no doubt

about the fact that there is a role for the committee, but the role of a special, joint or standing committee is not to paddle about the edges of the problem. It seems to me this is just what the motion is suggesting. The committee has to jump into the deep water where all the action is right now. When that time comes, I hope Conservative members of the committee will know how to swim.
I really wonder why the Indian people of Canada would want such a special joint committee poking about in their problems and concerns. Why should they place any particular trust or confidence in the work of such a committee as the one proposed in the Conservative motion? If they did not have trust and confidence in its work, there would be very good, historical reasons for that. We would be able to understand if that were the case. If Indian leaders and their people said to us, "Thanks, but we really do not need your inquiry or your special joint committee", we could understand this reaction.
I should like to refer to the year 1969, since it was brought up by hon. members opposite. On June 25, 1969, the government tabled its statement on Indian policy in the House of Commons. This document is referred to now as the Indian White Paper. That is a rather curious description, but one which carries with it a very useful message. Of course, at the time the statement was not perfectly understood.
A speech of the then minister of Indian affairs and northern development, which was given in Saskatchewan, was reprinted in Hansard dated December 1, 1969. The speech was entitled: "The Government Policy on Indians-What is the Debate About?" The minister went to some pains in that speech to explain what the statement was not, and then he went on to explain quite clearly what it was. It was a statement to be discussed. It indicated that the provinces should extend their services to Indians, and that the federal government should transfer funds to help the provinces do this. It is not my intention to go over all the proposals contained in that statement, but I should like to return to June 25, 1969, to see what was said in the House with reference to the work of a previous special joint committee. It was said that that committee had considerable input into the formulation of the 1969 statement.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), on June 25, 1969, in his address to the House, is reported at page 10583 of Hansard as saying the following:
I thank the minister for the statement he has made. There was a reminiscent tone to it. I recall during the last years of administration under the leadership of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) that a joint committee studied this issue. The wording of the report of that committee dealt with the winds of change which were blowing through the ranks of the Indian people of Canada. Many of the thoughts which the minister expressed in his statement were good thoughts, repeating the thoughts in the report of the committee.
We welcome the statement by the minister. It amounts to an acceptance of many proposals made by the Indian people through the years, and made by those who have worked on their behalf, in this party and elsewhere.
Following that, the spokesman for the New Democratic Party, the then hon. member for Skeena, Mr. Howard, said the following:
June 15, 1978

As I say, we listened with interest to what the minister said, because in a sense what he was saying was exactly the same thing as many Indian leaders and people have been saying for quite a number of years, and in a sense what he said was a reiteration of what many of us in this House have been saying for the last five or ten years.
The hon. member for Peace River and I had the opportunity in 1959, 1960 and 1961 of participating in the Joint Senate and House of Commons Committee on Indian Affairs, to which the hon. member for Peace River alluded, and the report of which committee contained the same ideas and concepts that the minister has now outlined. Even though it has taken some period of time to get a cabinet minister to agree with those concepts, it is still welcomed.
Now we have a special joint committee proposed to look at the Indian Act. The Indian people of Canada say that parliamentary committees do not listen very well. The hon. member said that what he heard from the Indian people was contained in the policy paper of 1969. When the Indian people saw the policy paper of 1969, they in fact told us quite clearly that that is not what they said at all, and that is not what they wanted. So what faith, what confidence, can they have in setting up another special joint committee to look into the provisions of the Indian Act? All members know that the statement of 1969 has been categorically rejected by the Indian people of Canada.
As I said, many of the proposals that flowed from the work of that committee are contained in that 1969 document. If we agree to the motion by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent today, I would have personal cause to be nervous about it. And I think that the Indian leaders of Canada would be more than nervous; they might be very hesitant about the results of the work of such a committee. In any event, before the committee ever gets its gear together there will either be a bill or a set of proposals to examine, and we will be very busy right here. There will be no time to flit from place to place within Canada, as the motion says, "sending for persons, papers and records and examining witnesses".
I must say that as parliamentarians we so often decry bureaucracy, but whenever we want to give the appearance of doing something we put forward a purely bureaucratic approach, and that 1 think is what we have in this motion today. -"Form another committee, take a look at the problem, listen to what people have to say and see if you can come up with something that is useful and valuable as a solution". This, from what I have heard today, is the answer of the Conservative party of Canada to an immensely complex and difficult issue.
The almost unanimous rejection by Indian leaders of the 1969 policy statements served as a major rallying force for Canada's Indian people. It has taught them and the government some valuable lessons. The government's reaction has been to drop the 1969 policy proposals. Chief Heber Maitland of Kitimat in northern British Columbia told a district manager's conference last year that the 1969 paper taught Indian people that they could no longer tolerate being treated like children of the government. It taught Indian leaders that they could and they should speak out in the best interests of their people, and it also taught the government to listen to Indian people.
Indian Affairs
It is the role of Indian leaders to inform the government about the needs of their people, and as a responsible government it is our role to listen and to take appropriate action. With respect to the revision of the Indian Act, I submit that that is precisely the process that is going on. Over the last several years it has been the policy of the government to involve Indian people in finding their own solutions to problems as they themselves perceive them. The Indian people are encouraged to define their own needs and to propose their own solutions. Indian involvement begins at the district level and then it extends to the national level.
As the minister suggested-and I agree entirely with him- the key to success in developing, implementing and maintaining a good working relationship between the department of Indian Affairs, on behalf of the federal government, and the Indian people is the effectiveness of local control and local government in Indian communities. Under the Indian Act the band council constitutes the authority to regulate life on the reserves. They make decisions that affect land and people within their boundaries, much the same way as do municipalities.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to enter into an extensive debate with the parliamentary secretary, but he did make one or two remarks that I would like to comment upon. He took issue with the remark of the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) regarding the setting up of the committee. I do not believe that the parliamentary secretary was in attendance at the committee meeting where this issue was raised. At that meeting there were representatives of the National Indian Brotherhood, and as a result of some of the comments that were made by some of the witnesses, the member for Prince George-Peace River put out this suggestion. It is interesting to note that the member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson), a member that sits on the government side, spoke very much in favour of setting up such a committee.
The parliamentary secretary also said that it appeared as though we on this side have just suddenly learned about the Indian people. I would suggest to him that it is because of this party back in 1973 that aboriginal rights were finally recognized by the government. The Indian people have a great deal of faith in our committee system. They come down quite often with their problems, and relate them to us. Unfortunately, the minister does not pay too much attention to what takes place in committee, but the ministers change so often that perhaps the minister is never in his portfolio long enough to really get a handle on the problems of the native people.
I am very pleased, Mr. Speaker, to participate in this debate this afternoon which calls for the setting up of a joint Senate and House of Commons committee to consider and report on the provisions of the Indian Act. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) made some excellent remarks in giving an overview of and historical background to the act.
6460

June 15, 1978
Indian Affairs
I came to Ottawa in 1972, and in the six years since that time I have been a member of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. During that time as a member of the committee and as a member of our caucus committee we have probably met with every native organization across Canada as well as many representatives of individual bands. During those meetings these people have expressed their concern about many problems such as health, housing, culture, economic development and survival as a people. They have expressed their concern about the Indian Act, which is basically the only protection they have. The representatives have indicated time and time again in the committee that they would like to see the Indian Act revised and updated, but they want an input into the act because it affects them so vitally.
The Indian people want to play a part in the preparation of a new act, but ultimately the responsibility of final consideration for the act and its passage rests with parliament. This is why our party feels that the setting up of such a committee as recommended in our motion today is so urgent. It would be a committee, as the motion states, that would travel throughout Canada to visit various communities where members are able to see at first hand and understand the problems of native people. I suggest that there are very few members in this House today who have any real appreciation of the problems that exist in the native communities.
A short time ago we had representatives of the National Indian Brotherhood before the standing committee as witnesses. I was impressed by the remarks of one witness in particular, Mike Martin, chief of Eel Ground Reserve in New Brunswick. I should like to quote a portion of his evidence in issue No. 3 of the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Indians Affairs and Northern Development for Thursday, May 4, 1978, at page 3:13, where he said:
We should have better recreation programs on our reserves to fight drugs and vandalism on the reserves.
As I stated a little while ago, people have been killed on reserves, dying because of other people shooting at another person. In fact, not too long ago, I lost my 21-year old son; he came home drunk one morning at five o'clock, he went down to his room, put a cartridge shell into a gun, stuffed it under his chin and blew his head right out. That is my experience about what has taken place on reserves in vandalism and drugs. I lost my son, not too long ago, on account ot that. When I say this is what is taking place, it is taking place. If some of you people could take time-I know you have quite a lot of travelling funds in your pocket, free travelling funds in your pocket-to go up to the reserves, spend more time and see exactly what is taking place on the reserves, you would know what is taking place. You would know how the people are suffering on the reserves-housing-anything else that has been mentioned here. Even the people of the Department of Indian Affairs, who are running the programs do not come up to see us and see what is taking place. All they say is, "We know what is taking place on your reserve."
I suggest the situation is critical, Mr. Speaker. I lay the blame on this government which over the years has adopted an attitude of paternalism and a program of assimilation. The government has failed to listen to the voice of the Indian people and to the Indian leaders who express the collective views of their people.

If I had time I should like to read a letter from Chief David Ahenakew to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), a copy of which came across my desk this morning. He is concerned about the situation in Saskatchewan and issues a warning about the possible consequences. I know Chief Ahenakew, who is doing and has done an excellent job in Saskatchewan. The letter that he sent to the Prime Minister, of which I think many members have a copy, is a warning, a warning that must be heeded.
I recall talking to Chief Ahenakew a couple of years ago when he said, in effect: "We do not want any handouts, we do not want your welfare; welfare is destroying our people. What we want is opportunity, encouragement, the responsibility to make decisions on our own." He indicated that mistakes would be made, but then the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has made a great many mistakes. He looked to the future, a future when native people would be self-reliant and able through their own endeavours to take care of themselves. They are not looking for handouts. How can they become self-reliant, Mr. Speaker? It can only be done through adequate education, adequate training and economic development.
I should like to spend a few minutes on the subject of economic development. A few years ago the government set up an Indian economic development fund. The concept was based on the white paper of 1969 and was established in 1970. It was funded with some $50 million to be used over a period of five years and basically was to fund small, viable businesses to a maximum of $50,000. It was also to act as a lever for funds from other agencies such as DREE.
The facts of what happened are well documented in the committee hearings of 1977 and in the opposition day debate of June 22 of that year. The Indian economic development fund has not been a success, Mr. Speaker. A study carried out in 1976 by the firm of Woods, Gordon & Co. indicated in part:
It is our opinion that, in dealing with individuals and small enterprises, the fund has had some measure of success. However, in large complex projects, the fund's performance in relation to its original mandate has been a dismal failure.
The fund was intended to be used on projects to a maximum of $50,000. I suggest that through the ambitions of members of the department it was expanded to include such large enterprises, to mention only one, as The Pas shopping centre. This is a project which started at some $6 million and, with an over-run, ended up in excess of $8.3 million. The over-run was primarily due to the requirements of the Department of Public Works with respect to the structure of the building.
I could cite many other glaring examples which are well documented. Evidence given in committee will indicate that from the inception of the program until we held our committee meetings in 1977 the total number of projects was 2,577, yet they only created 4,722 jobs-less than two jobs per project.
It is interesting to note that with respect to larger projects of half a million dollars or more the fund invested some $45 million, or between 40 per cent and 50 per cent of the total funds available, yet that $45 million created only 58 jobs. At
June 15, 1978

the committee hearings we learned that every one of the projects costing over $500,000 was in financial difficulty.
This government has failed miserably in attempting to create economic self-sufficiency for native people in Canada. It has also, unfortunately, created doubts in the minds of many of the ability of the native people to handle their own economic development. The evidence will show, however, that in most instances the smaller projects were successful, particularly those under $100,000. Had officials of the department kept within their mandate and funded smaller projects, the program would have been generally successful.
The Indian Act has a bearing on the economic future of the Indian people. Despite what the parliamentary secretary has to say, I visualize this committee as being similar to the Special Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs which travelled extensively, gained first-hand knowledge about our penitentiary system and tabled an excellent report. This proposed committee could do the same. It could see at first hand some of the projects funded by the Indian economic development fund. It could see the housing conditions. It could examine health, listen to presentations and receive suggestions and recommendations from the band level.
I appreciate that there is not much general agreement among the native community with respect to changes in the act, but studies have been carried out and are carried out through funding of the NIB by the government and I believe the problem areas within the act have at least been identified.
As the hon. member for Lambton-Kent pointed out earlier, we are presently in a debate and a dialogue on national unity. We concern ourselves about bilingualism and multiculturalism and yet we are overlooking the indigenous people of our country, the people who were here long before the white man. I suggest that a committee such as we have proposed in this motion would receive wide media coverage in its travels. It would perhaps make Canadians aware of a matter which at the present time they know little about.
Such a committee would also make members of parliament sensitive to the problems that exist. It would enable them to consider constructively and intelligently a new act, an act that hopefully will be one out of which new policies may evolve, for example, policies for local government based on input from the people who are concerned so that without bureaucratic interference they will be able to build their own future as you and I, Mr. Speaker, have been able to do.
I see that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. In closing I would simply like to say that I urge the government to give serious consideration to what we feel is an excellent and constructive motion, one which could do a very fine job in making decisions on a new Indian Act.
