subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I enter the debate this evening on the motion proposed by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), not with the intention of criticizing the hon. member because my association with him in the past four years as a fellow member of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development is such that I hold him in high esteem. Rather, I want him to know, and I want the House to know, that my concern is with the mechanics of the motion.
My riding of Coast Chilcotin has within its borders more than 30 Indian reservations; some are close to towns and cities while others are to be found in very remote locations. The hon. member proposes that the parliamentary committee to be established should go to all places in Canada to sit down and hold discussions. This may work out well in those areas which are close to cities and towns but I would be most disturbed to think that we might decide to take 15 members of this House and an equal number from the other place and pour them into these various remote areas. It may work well enough in the cities but I could name places in my riding in which we could
80045-42(4

June 15, 1978
Indian Affairs
face some quite remarkable scenes and Heaven knows what actions.
I mention, for example, Oweekeno, where a band is situated right up at the top of Rivers Inlet. I wonder how the hon. member would propose to bring a group of pin-striped clad characters from Ottawa into such an area. The only way to get in there is by a small float plane, probably with a maximum capacity of three or four. We would spend all day bringing people into places like Oweekeno.
Another place which comes to mind is Nemeihia Valley in the heart of the Chilcotins. I am sure the hon. member knows of the places I am talking about because he does his homework and knows British Columbia as well as I do. I want also to mention Nazko. These are areas which rarely see many white people. Indeed, they may see the odd trapper or prospector, occasionally a rancher or member of parliament going in there to do his best.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
As a consequence, I cannot picture this group of individuals coming from Ottawa to go into, for instance, Nazko and Nemeihia Valley to sit down and say to the chief and council: "Okay, we are here for five hours; you have ten minutes in which to have your say and then bring on all the rest." These people have not grown up with that kind of life. They would not understand the kind of parliamentary committee system under which we operate here. We are caught up in this cocoon where we jump from one place to another to attend the various committees on which we serve. We are allowed ten minutes to ask questions. How could you expect to operate such a system in these remote areas where the people are not accustomed to speaking in front of large groups like ours, particularly when they are not even used to speaking to white people?
I believe that the NIB, nationally and provincially, have managed to get through to their people. The various groups with which 1 deal all the time are men and women who are as close as it is possible to get to the native people. Are we going to abandon their efforts and say: "No, I'm sorry, you have done a good job but we want to find out a bit more on our own"? How can we sit down with a group of people who are totally unaccustomed to our ways and give them five minutes to speak to us? They won't say a word. They will just sit there and look at us. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent knows, having gone into these areas, that you have to go in and sit down and personally talk to the chief and council. You get more out of that kind of action than you ever will by bringing in a committee. I understand what the hon. member wants to do and I admire him for it, but the mechanics he proposes to employ would just put a stop to it all. That is what disturbs me so much.
Now, we have talked about the remote areas. I am very fortunate in my riding to have a number of very advanced Indian reservations. I don't mind naming them-I think they should be named. They are an honour to their people, an honour to all the people of Canada. For instance, there is the

Sliammon band, on the outskirts of Powell River, my own hometown. They have done a tremendous job in the last few years and are well ahead, thanks, perhaps, to the industries which surround them. In Sechelt, just to the south on the sunshine coast, there is a wonderful group who have done an excellent job-it is close to the city. I could move on and name, for example, the Squamish band which the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington) represents. A portion of the band is to be found in my riding. These are areas which would understand the system and could sit down with a parliamentary committee. They are very experienced in politics and would win the battle over us any day-something which I am sure the hon. member for Lambton-Kent already knows.
But let us not forget that the great majority of the Indian people in Canada do not live close to cities. That is the point which disturbs me so much. As well-intentioned as the proposal may be, Mr. Speaker, I do not feel that such a committee could do the job that the National Indian Brotherhood or all the provincial bodies can do. I would far rather see an opportunity afforded us to keep on with the business we are doing today, meeting with Mr. Starblanket, meeting with Mr. Manuel and those who have been before them. This is the route we have taken and I believe it is the route we should stay with. Otherwise we must have some idea how we can explain to, say, a chief up in Kingcome Inlet: "I am sorry, Chief. You wanted to make a presentation to the B.C. Indian Chiefs but Ottawa says that won't work. We have a new committee coming out here. We are going to bring you some senators and members of parliament. You will be given five minutes to tell them your story"-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext: How about 15?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
Well, 15 is not enough. These people have suffered for a hundred years from the presence of the white man, and now you propose to give them 15 minutes to explain their cause. I am sure the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) really did not mean that. We have to give them the time they need. They do not talk in a hurry as we have learned to do because our time is limited. We are talking with native people who are accustomed to a very slow and easy way. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent knows that, and so does the hon. member for Moose Jaw. They know what happens when you go among the native people. One does not hurry things, you just sit down. It may take a whole hour just to get an introduction but this is their way of life.
As I say, I respect what the hon. member wants to do but the mechanics just will not permit it to happen as he suggests. 1 just foresee our running into terrible confusion where, instead of getting the information we need and desire, we will get nothing. Some of these Indian people are quite timid. They just sit back and refuse to say a word. I would far rather see us carry on as we have been doing, listening to Mr. Starblanket and the other Indian representatives.
I heard what the minister had to say this afternoon. We do have a committee which is studying the question. We under-
June 15, 1978

stand one another. We are working on something we all believe in. 1 have great respect for the hon. member who proposed this motion, as I have for all members of the committee. I honestly believe the Indians realize we are trying to do something. But we have the Indian Act. It is a horrible act. It has been in effect for over one hundred years and it is about time we changed it. But let us do it in the way we can do it best, by bringing in representatives of the native people and letting them tell us what they would like to see done. They should not be limited to ten minutes. Witnesses have come a long way. They should be given hours, if necessary, in which to talk to us.
What have we done to our native people in the course of a hundred years? We have pushed them down and never given them a chance. They cannot tell their story in half an hour. These people have not been brought up in a TV culture. They are talking about trying to get back where they belong.
Although I understand what the hon. member for Lambton-Kent is getting at, I feel that the mechanics involved with his proposal would not fit into the program. Frankly, what I am seeking is greater association and confrontation-and I think that is the right word to use-with our native people. As an individual member of parliament I am prepared to continue doing what I have been doing in the four years since my election here. I have been sitting down with these people, spending my time with them and bringing their problems to the minister. I have had excellent results, as I am sure have other hon. members. We are moving in the right direction, but let us not abandon completely the native representatives who come here time and time again. Different speakers this afternoon have been saying that we are going to be throwing them out and telling Mr. Starblanket and other representatives to get lost because we do not need them. That is not the way to proceed. I respect what the hon. member is trying to do, but I feel that if we throw native leaders out, we will get into a very serious situation. We must not tell them to get lost. We must stay with them.
When we talk about Indian rights and land claims, we must stay with the people themselves but we must get information from them. How can we as a group of 30 or more-it does not say in the motion how many there might be; there could be 100 of us for all I know; I do not know what the Senate representation might be-get across to people in remote areas? That bothers me. I do not think we will. That is why I would be much happier if the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, the hon. member for Moose Jaw and myself could bring people here to Ottawa and give them more time. I am sure those hon. members would agree with me. We are ten minutes ourselves into Heaven knows what.
Sometimes I wonder if we really know where we are going, because we have ourselves tied into a cocoon of committees. The people of Canada want to speak, and I am referring to both Indian and white. However, they are not being given that
Indian Affairs
opportunity. The rules are not just made by the government. We have a system here.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
I notice that the hon. member is applauding. I am glad because I think he understands that we must get down to the basics and understand that we are dealing with native people who are not accustomed to the jet set lifestyle we have here, where everything is done by the clock, we are hit with gavels all over the place and where there are bells ringing. We in this place are the crazy ones! We are letting ourselves be tied into things where everything is done in five minute intervals, or more or less, depending upon what we are dealing with.
Let us sit down and analyse this thing properly. I think the minister was quite right when he said that we are negotiating. We are negotiating well. There have been great accomplishments in the past few years. I am glad to know this, and I am sure all hon. members are; but one thing which will really cause us problems and which I do not think will be settled by having this special committee is that hunting and fishing limits will be involved. Those are crucial issues out in British Columbia. The northern gas pipeline will be involved. I know that the hon. member for Lambton-Kent knows this because we have both been members of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. We know what the B.C. chiefs are saying. As a member of that committee I have a responsibility for trying to get a message to them. There are many things in the Indian Act, but a committee of white men cannot deal with them effectively.
In this House this evening is one of our hon. colleagues who knows what this is all about. I do not know whether he will be speaking tonight. 1 refer to the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand). He knows, and I feel very honoured to be associated and working with my colleague. I only hope that he gets an opportunity to speak tonight and to tell the story as he has heard it from his people. We are looking into a mirror, but has anybody ever wondered what is being reflected? I do not think we are getting the real story, and that is why I reject what the hon. member for Lambton-Kent is proposing. I think he has an excellent idea, but its time will come later.
I think the body to deal with these matters should be the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, but I hope native people will be given permission to present themselves without any interference from Ottawa because they have been charging Ottawa with interfering all through the years.
I was born on the west coast. I have lived all my life among native people as well as with my own white people. I know the feeling and the stories of the people. I do not want to leave the impression that I am trying to destroy what the hon. member is proposing, but I feel that the mechanics of his motion will not permit what he is asking. I think we should stay with the system we have had. I think we should try to develop that system further. I do want to see the National Indian Brotherhood carry on with what it is doing. I would like to see it spend

June 15, 1978
Indian Affairs
more time with us, and I feel that the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development is the committee to deal with native questions. However, let there be equal participation. If we do not have that, later it will be said that the whites took over and "did it to us again". I do not think there is a member in this House who would want to have that thrown at him. I understand that there could be hon. members here who represent constituencies which have no native groups, but there are close to three dozen bands within my riding. I must think of those people as I make my decision here tonight.
I feel that I cannot go along with the motion presented by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent because I feel I would be letting down my native friends within my riding who want to get their story across. They do not feel they can get it across by coming to a city or by having a group come to speak for them. That is not their way of life, and I do not think we should impose our way upon them at this crucial moment when we are going to make revisions to the Indian Act. It is about time we made those revisions.
I am not going to take any more time. I think I have put my message across, and I hope my hon. friends understand what I have been saying.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in the debate on the motion moved by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) I can say that never in my short tenure in this House have I seen three government members scratch so hard to speak against a motion. They are scratching from the very bottom. I think they are talking out of both sides of their mouths. If any of the hon. members opposite who have spoken today were to come across a mukluk, I do not think they would know whether to eat it or wear it. That is about how much knowledge they have of Indian people.
Since arriving here in Ottawa four short years ago I have been a member of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I represent about 35 Indian reserves. There are more treaty Indians in my riding than in the riding of many other members in this House, and I think I speak with a little bit of authority. I have spent some 32 years living and working with Indian people. Hon. members opposite talk about our great standing committee to which everybody can come. Witnesses appear, we hear them and so forth, but this government is not prepared to meet the Indians on their own ground. The government always wants Indian people to come here to Ottawa. The government wants to control Indian people by remote control.
The hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. Pearsall) spoke about going to reserves in pin-stripe suits. I expect that that is the way he approaches the Indian people. He does not really have an honest feeling about how to deal with the Indian people and with Indian problems.
Time and time again I have seen witnesses appear before the parliamentary committee where they get 20 minutes or half an hour to present their briefs. What action does the standing
[Mr. Pearsall.)
committee ever take on those briefs? Not one darn bit of action. The brief is presented and that is it; everybody goes away smiling and shaking hands, and the brief gathers dust like so many studies done by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development over the years. The Indian people are studied to death.
I think we would get a tremendous support from the Indian people across Canada for a standing committee which would go out and meet the Indian people on their own terms and on their own ground, instead of them having to come down to Ottawa and meet the fellows in the pin-stripe suits. That is how much regard these fellows have for the Indian people.
Let me say, Mr. Speaker, in speaking in favour of the motion, that the Indian people at the community level, at the band level in remote locations, and so on, are the first people of Canada, and we must remember that. But this government is treating them as if they were the last people in Canada. To date the federal government has consistently imposed on the Indian people its policies and programs with little regard for the needs and concerns of the Indians. Policies which originate here in Ottawa dribble through numerous bureaucratic hands before reaching the Indian communities. Of course, when those policies take that route they are bound to fail. The reasons are numerous and obvious to us down here in Ottawa. Unfortunately, they are probably not as obvious to people in the remote locations.
Let me just recount what has taken place in the department in my short tenure of four years here. Today the minister gave us the impression that all is well, everything is going fine, that there is continuity in the work of the department. Let me tell you how much continuity there is in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, just one of the departments with which the Indian people must deal. In the past four years there have been so many changes in the structure and organization of the department that it is very doubtful that there is any continuity in policy for more than two months at a time. We have witnessed in the past four years the appointment of three different ministers in charge of Indian affairs. We still do not have a minister who is quite dry behind the ears in so far as that department is concerned. He has been here for a few months and already he is the expert who knows how to solve all the problems. I wish him well. We have had two different deputy ministers and we have had a change of assistant deputy ministers, all in four short years. And yet the department expects the Indian people to have continuity and control at the band level, to know what is going on and to run their affairs properly.
Let me tell hon. members what happened in the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in four years because of the change in administration here in Ottawa. There has been a reorganization of the department, which means that nothing works for the next six months. There has been realignment in the department, which means that nothing works for another six months because everybody is shuffling papers around and moving people from desk to desk. In the meantime, people back in the reserves are not receiving the attention they
June 15, 1978

deserve. Then lo and behold, in comes a new ADM. What is he going to do? He comes up with a program called "Fine Tuning". Again that program changes everything around. Now the latest program is called "Fusion".
Let me tell the House that all that change in the past few years has meant to us here in Ottawa and to the Indian people mass confusion, not fusion. That is exactly what it has meant. One wonders how workable all these activities have made the department. One can be quite sure that all these goings on have only frustrated the Indian people back in the areas where the programs and the moneys have finally dribbled down. As I have mentioned before, these activities frustrated the Indian people who are trying to develop their communities within the confines of a confused and confusing organization, and this is being perpetuated right down through the system.
Indian affairs policies cannot possibly reflect the broad range of cultural, economic and geographical differences of the Indian communities across this country. That is why we must have a committee travelling across the country and getting the feeling of the grass roots people. There is a place and a job for the National Indian Brotherhood and there is a place and a job for the various provincial organizations, such as the Manitoba Indian Brotherhood and the FSI. There are pressure groups and they have their job to do. But there is also a job for the parliamentary committee to hear recommendations of people other than those I just mentioned, such as the NIB and the MIB. They do a good job but they have so much work to do that sometimes they cannot even get to some of the locations that a special standing committee could reach. Decisions cannot be made without due consultation with the Indian people.
The thinking of the department here is that it could develop a program here in Ottawa and send it out to the communities, but only the department can administer the program. This year officials of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development have said in Ottawa in the committee that they have reduced their spending by 3 per cent. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, what that means to the Indian reserves back at the community level where the band council is trying to administer a program and develop band government? It means a reduction of 17 per cent at the band level by the time it dribbles all the way down to them. Their head office is not suffering. It is the band, the people whom the department is supposed to serve, who are suffering. They are the ones who will lose 17 per cent and who will have to lay off 50 per cent of the people to carry out the program. If the program is not carried out properly, department officials say to them: "Apparently you cannot handle this so we will have to step in and send some of our people in to run the program. You people just stand aside. We know how to do it because we have all the experts who know how to handle Indian people and how to do this work".
Recognition by the federal government of the crucial need for Indian input in the determination of programs was not given until the mid-1960s. The formation of regional Indian advisory councils occurred in the late 1960s. The objective of
Indian Affairs
the government was to provide the Indian people with a consulting role with regard to policy and in the area of amendments to the Indian Act. That the government never seriously offered the Indian people more than token gestures of involvement was fully demonstrated in their 1969 policy white paper on Indians. The government's idea of the role of Indians regarding policy was simply that they would administer on the local level policies designed by the department. In fact, the white paper made an absolute mockery of the consultation process that had supposedly occurred.
What the bands want and are after today at the band level is band government. They want to be able to control what goes on in their communities. They are sick and tired of someone arriving in their communities in the morning and leaving at night-the 24-hour experts, I call them. They arrive, lay out some particular program and leave, and that is probably the last the band sees of them. Of course, the individual who arrives from the department does not leave any funds to administer the particular program. He feels the Indian people at the band level should be doing this for nothing because a lot of them are receiving welfare. He feels they should just do the administration work for nothing. The department fails to recognize that when it brings someone in from the regional office the money required is coming from a program, and that money should be going to the Indian people. The government had obviously not been listening to the Indian people because they have been saying this for quite some time, and this is something we do not hear at this level. We just do not get this information.
I sometimes feel that the ideas presented by the Indian people never really get past the regional level, if they ever get that far, for the simple reason that there are too many people in the department who are protecting their own jobs and do not want too much autonomy for some of these bands. Of course, that could be argued, but that is exactly what I have found during the 32 years I have been working with and for the Indian people in northern Manitoba.
When this 1969 white paper came down the Indian people were angry. They certainly felt, and understandably so, betrayed by a government which had made a great pretence of consulting with the Indians. The problems of today can be related to the fact that the Indian people do not trust this government. That is why they are leery of even discussing some things with the government. Trust is something that has to be developed, and it cannot be developed overnight. Trust is something that is developed through years and years of working with these people.
The Indian associations insisted that resources be made available to enable band councils to determine local needs and to run their respective communities. The Indian associations have consistently maintained that only a grass roots approach will work for the Indian people. This requires a decentralization of the top heavy Indian Affairs structure, and a true partnership between the Department of Indian Affairs and the

June 15, 1978
Indian Affairs
band councils. A far more flexible approach to policy formation is also necessary.
However, not until 1974 were band councils given serious recognition. The band council was finally viewed as a distinct political body, legally elected with a number of important functions. The band could raise and spend funds, could hire band staff, contract with other levels of government and administer a variety of programs. However, the programs were and are still predominantly those designed by the Department of Indian Affairs. Although the government's intentions seemed laudable on paper, the Indian people were still rather concerned, and they are now, about any real input they had in the development of their communities. This is a very strong feeling.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and an increasingly wide array of other federal agencies still dominate the situation at the band level. They make plans and the numerous agents fly in and out of the reserve, foisting their plans on communities in a largely uncoordinated fashion. The band councils have numerous local concerns to deal with, and it is unrealistic to expect that any and all band councils can deal with all these agents and plans in a reasonably coherent manner. A major goal of the Indian people remains that of realizing a community development plan which ultimately results in autonomous, self-sufficient communities.
I would like now to deal briefly with education in particular communities. In many of the communities we know that education has been in the limelight for several years, simply because of the approach this government has taken toward education of the Indian people. Under the terms of the Indian Act, and as stated in various treaties, the federal government has legal responsibility for Indian education.
Traditionally the government's concept of education for the Indian people has been dangerously narrow in scope, and consequently most ineffectual. The government's attempt to assimilate Indians through education has had numerous disastrous effects, not the least of which has been high drop-out rates and general disdain for a system which is alien and rejects their own cultural values.
For more than a hundred years Indian education has been directed and controlled by churches and/or the federal government. Generations of Indian people will recall being shipped out long distances as children to attend a variety of residential schools, mission schools, boarding schools and industrial schools. The sense of helplessness and loneliness experienced by children cut off from their families and communities remains a blight on our history. Every attempt was made to negate their cultural identity and the values with which they had been raised. Their language rights were eroded by teachers who discouraged the children from speaking their own mother tongue. They were subjected to literature that depicted their culture and values in a distorted and often negative fashion. The fact that Indian people have made valuable contributions to history was a fact simply overlooked by their educators. The lack of well qualified teachers and the often

dismal and inadequate facilities only compounded the problem.
Well aware of the failures, the federal government decided in the late 1940s to take a more active interest in the education of Indian children. The major objective of that interest, however, was to bring Indian children into the mainstream of the dominant society. The policy was that of enforced assimilation, with a resultant loss of all Indian cultural identity. Once again parental and community wishes were entirely overlooked. This system which has denied the Indian people any control over the lives of their children has, of course, resulted in a massive failure.
Once again the federal government was faced with the failure of its educational policies. In the late 1960s the department decided that some participation by Indian people in the education of their children was required. The notion that their children needed to be integrated into the mainstream was still dominating the department's policies and was, in fact, even further reinforced. The trend was now to integrate children into the provincial school systems. Federal-provincial contracts were formulated without consulting the parents or the Indian people generally. Indian participation was evidently no more than a token gesture. It was the Indian people themselves that initiated the most important developments in education, beginning in the late 1960s.
I see that my time is drawing to a close, Mr. Speaker, but I have one letter here from Oxford House and I would like to refer to one small part of it. This explains why we should have a committee able to travel to these reserves. This letter concerns a school that closed down because the roads were in such terrible condition that the school bus could no longer use them. The letter is signed by Chief Jack Grieves of Oxford House and four of his councillors. Today that school is still not open and the children are not attending because of the policies of this federal Indian affairs department.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity of speaking for a few moments on the motion of the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes). I do not suggest that I support the motion, but I certainly welcome the opportunity to speak on it and to make one or two comments about the speech of the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith).
For him to portray himself as the only one who represents a large number of Indian bands or status Indians is an utter falsehood. We have many members on this side of the House who represent large numbers of Indian bands. My own constituency alone has 4,000 status Indians and about 12 Indian bands. For the hon. member to make the suggestion that he or certain members on his side of the House are the only people to have an opportunity to visit band councils and to meet with the native people is certainly unjustified.
I want to pay special tribute to the parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Peel-Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Milne), who

has had an opportunity to meet on one of the Indian reserves in Algoma riding, the Mississauga reserve, with chiefs from several bands to discuss special problems that affect bands throughout the Algoma-Manitoulin area, because he certainly did an excellent job. Contrary to what the hon. member for Churchill said, he was able to effect many changes that were raised at the meeting.
The hon. member for Churchill talks about mass confusion in the Department of Indian Affairs. I cannot think of anything that would prejudice the consultations and negotiations which are going on now between the National Indian Brotherhood and the department with regard to amendments to the Indian Act than to send out a committee across the country before these negotiations and consultations are completed. The hon. member for Churchill portrays practically every employee of the Department of Indian Affairs as a blackhearted wretch. He did not actually use those words, but he as much as said that every individual in the department does not have the best interests of the Indian bands at heart. That is a false concept because, surely, we have many dedicated public servants who are doing an excellent job working with band councils and Indian groups to improve the situation on the Indian reserves. It certainly does not take very long for the chiefs and councillors and band council members to tell you which ones are which.
The motion before the House is to set up a special committee to consider and report on the Indian Act and what revisions or amendments should be made in that regard. In 1968-69 there was very extensive consultation across the country which involved the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras). It was a very valuable exercise, but the important thing now is for the department and the minister to have consultations with the National Indian Brotherhood and other groups across the country and to bring before parliament the proposed amendments resulting from those consultations. If you were to send a committee out across the country at this stage, it would only negate those consultations and confuse the issue rather than result in constructive amendments to the act.
I would like now to put the problem in its proper perspective. A few years ago an incident occurred in my constituency where many young people aged 18, 19 and 20 years suddenly found that they could vote in the federal election at the time the provincial and federal law for voting age was changed from 21 to 18. I had presented a private member's bill to lower the voting age for status Indians in the elections of band councils and chiefs. The bill was on the order paper for a couple of years. I believe that practically everybody in the country, including most members of the National Indian Brotherhood, band councillors and certainly young people who are deprived of voting at age 18, 19 or 20 at the present time, would like to see that amendment become law.
The National Indian Brotherhood has made it very clear- and I have received feedback to this effect-that they do not want to open the act up on a piecemeal basis, making changes here and there with only one or two changes actually being
Indian Affairs
effected. This, in effect, is what we would be doing if we were to pass an amendment like that of the private member's bill. The National Indian Brotherhood wants to negotiate with the department and the minister amendments to the entire act.
This afternoon the hon. member for Lambton-Kent portrayed the Indian bands and Indian reserves by laying out all their difficulties, the social and economic problems with which they are faced. Well, we are working to improve the situation, and if hon. members will look back just eight or ten years, the period of time that 1 have been a member in this House, they will see some dramatic and impressive changes that have occurred, at least in my constituency. Perhaps the most impressive in that regard is the kind of leadership which has developed to make this progress, to provide for social amenities on the Indian reserves. It seems to me that this leadership has sprung up because in the old days it was simply a case of the band council acting as an advisory group to the Indian agent who ran the whole show.
Today, however, we have Indian bands operating many programs such as housing, education, economic development, direct employment, nursing homes, parks and recreational facilities. There has been a tremendous step forward in this area over the past eight or ten years, and the band councils have proven their ability to operate extensive and complicated programs that are often much more complicated, at least in my area, than those operated by a municipal council of comparable size. We would be remiss if we did not point out that kind of progress.
The area to be most concerned about in the future is economic development, especially for the remote reserves where it is difficult for band members to find employment. This has to be a chief concern of the department, the minister and all of us, because if people do not have job opportunities the system breaks down.
I want to congratulate the Indian bands on the facilities they are providing for their band council members. A few weeks ago I had an opportunity to attend the official opening of a recreational and cultural facility at the Sagamok reserve. There was also a new band administrative centre with firehall and police station, an excellent facility. Other bands throughout the Algoma-Manitoulin area have provided equivalent facilities as well.
Another reserve I would like to mention is the one adjacent to Sault Ste. Marie, where the Batchewana band have built an excellent recreational complex, administrative centre and industrial park where many small light service industries are locating. This not only provides a tax base for that band but provides jobs. There is much progress being made, but we have a considerable way to go.
As for the economic development aspect, when we get around to making amendments to the Indian Act I think it is very important that we provide power for band councils to be able to lease property on the reserve. I understand from what the minister has said that it is the plan that band councils be

June 15, 1978
Indian Affairs
given the power, substantially, to lease land without having a surrender vote, although if they actually sold land they would need to have a surrender vote. That is one of the important issues that was raised with the parliamentary secretary at the reserve meeting held in Mississauga last November.
Another thing that we want to see established is postsecondary education. In northeastern Ontario we have been watching a battle to ensure that funding is provided for post-secondary education this fall. There is some concern that when we amend the Indian Act, whatever regulation or statute is established will ensure that post-secondary education receives the same consideration that public and elementary school education receives now. The uncertainty there is about this is a great hardship to the people involved and it is undesirable at a time of high unemployment. I think it is important that the matter be clarified, as the minister has indicated it will be in the near future.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, the motion before us to establish a special committee to roam the country at a time when consultations are taking place is premature. I do not think the motion should pass. The minister has indicated that he hopes to bring in amendments to the act, perhaps next year, and to get substantial agreement with the National Indian brotherhood later this year. That is the procedure to follow. The bill would come before parliament after agreement has been reached with the national association and various representatives of native groups could appear before the committee. That is the positive, constructive and least confusing way to proceed on this most important matter.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the minister's contribution to this debate earlier in the day, there is no doubt in my mind that the reference of the Indian Act to a special parliamentary committee as proposed by my colleague the hon. member for Lamb-ton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) is even more of a necessity than I believed.
It is obvious from the minister's remarks that if this act is to be amended with the full participation of the Indian community, they must be provided with a forum where they can make their views known, where all aspects can be dealt with, not in camera but under the full scrutiny of public opinion. It is to be hoped that this would force the minister, his advisers and members of the government to give the revision the priority it should have and which they have denied it to date.
This afternoon the minister scoffed at the idea of a committee such as this and derided its potential value. He did not think the Indian Act needed further study. He said that no other matter has been studied so much, unless it be the constitution. I would say to the minister, as he probably knows, that after a year and a half of urgings and motions from this side of the House, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has finally agreed to set up a special parliamentary committee to deal with constitutional matters. I hope the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) will see

the wisdom of that move by the Prime Minister, belated though it is, and that he will reverse his position on the motion before us.
Sir, the minister said that he would rather build on the work that had been done prior to the breakdown of the NIB-cabinet joint committee. He went on to outline what had actually been achieved but then treated us to a review of the various matters which had been dealt with, the various attempts that had been made, which in his own words had foundered.
In lieu of a special parliamentary committee working on this necessary revision, the minister plans to soldier on by himself, and his closing remarks were: "I would hope to have some proposals by the fall". Pious hopes by the minister are no substitute for action and involvement-no longer good enough for the native people who have had to bear the inconsistencies and bureaucratic strictures of the Indian Act for far too long. They must be provided with a new forum, a special forum in which to make their views known, and a special parliamentary committee could perform that function.
I want to deal particularly with the discriminatory clauses in the Indian Act, clauses which relate to band membership and particularly as they apply to Indian women. The minister mentioned these clauses. He said in response to a question from the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) that he would tell him and the House how this matter-these discriminatory clauses-would be dealt with, but then he never did.
I should like to refer the minister and the House to a special publication put out in April of this year by the Advisory Council on the Status of Women entitled "Indian Women and the Law in Canada: Citizens Minus". The preface reads as follows:
When native women in Canada realized that there was no documentation of the discrimination against us we requested the assistance of the Advisory Council on the Status of Women. We asked them to work with us jointly in our efforts to prepare this documentation.
The result was the booklet I have referred to. Later in this publication there appears the following passage:
For one hundred and nine years Indian women in Canada have been subject to a law which discriminates against them on the grounds of race, sex and marital status.
For the past nine years various attempts have beem made to revise the Indian Act in order to rid the act of its discriminatory clauses. To date, none of this has met with success. As my colleague the hon. member for Lambton-Kent has already outlined, there was the federal government white paper in 1969 which was received with outrage and hostility by the Indian community.
Several years later, in 1974, a committee of the National Indian Brotherhood under the chairmanship of Harold Cardinal, then president of the Alberta Indian Association, prepared a draft revised act which recommended that discrimination be removed from the act and that Indian women not lose status on marriage.
In 1975, a joint committee of the government and the NIB was set up to revise the Indian Act and the whole issue of
June 15, 1978

Indian women and band membership became a political football in their negotiations. So ineffective was the work of that committee that the NIB withdrew from it this spring, claiming that it was a charade and that they had not received one major decision from the government in the entire time they had been working on it. Its attempts, as the minister said, "had foundered".
I have always believed-indeed, I have spoken about this before in the House-that Indians themselves should have the primary input into any redraft of the Indian Act. That is why I put so much hope into the work of that joint committee and why I regret its collapse. Now some other vehicle must be found which will enable us to remove, once and for all, the very real discrimination that exists against Indian women.
I have met with many groups of Indian women on this subject and others, but particularly on this subject. I have been greatly encouraged and amazed by the solidarity of both status and non-status women in the way in which they are working together to resolve their problems as women. I have met individual Indians who are deeply affected by the injustice of the Indian Act. I think of women like Mary Two-Axe Early of the Caughnawaga reserve who told me, sadly but indeed angrily, that it is easier for the dogs to be buried on the reserve than it is for her, a full-blooded Indian who has been stripped of her status. So while committees are formed, talk and collapse, the Indian women are forced to sit in frustration.
The Advisory Council on the Status of Women in the report I have mentioned said this at page 91 about the now defunct joint committee:
The NIB in the present joint government-Indian negotiations to revise the Indian Act, has refused to allow status or non-status native women's organizations to be represented in these negotiations. Curiously the federal government does not see anything at all amiss with the fact that the NIB can unilaterally make such a decision. As "Indians" meant only males to the governments in the past, so it is today.
And, as that report further points out:
This denial of the human rights of Indian women on the part of both the government and the NIB has been compounded by the fact that this same government has carefully excluded any possible recourse in law by removing the Indian Act from the reach of the new Human Rights Act which came into force on March 1, 1978. Indian women have nowhere to turn and are denied the basic human rights enjoyed by other Canadians.
After nine years of talk about changing the law, Indian women are still suffering from its discriminatory clauses. The best known of these is section 12(1 )(b). 1 am sure as many members realize that infamous clause states that, upon marriage to a white man, an Indian woman must leave the reservation, may not own property on the reserve, must give up any property she does own, cannot inherit any property, cannot take part in band business, cannot have her children recognized as Indian, is prevented from returning to live with her family even if she is poverty-stricken, ill, widowed or divorced, and finally loses the right to burial on the reserve.
Canadians, native and non-native alike, can and have been concerned about this one section of the law which most people
Indian Affairs
in the country consider discriminatory. But what about all the other sections that have not generated a hue and cry, the ones that we have not raised a fuss about, probably because many of us are unaware that they exist? That whole section of the Indian Act which deals with definition and registration of Indians, sections 5 to 17, needs close scrutiny to see just how much injustice exists for both men and women.
For example, the 1951 revision introduced a new system of registration on band lists. I will not go into the problems this created when many people were left off the lists because of inadequate and faulty registration procedures. But suffice to say that persons, men and women, who were legally entitled to be included were left off. That particular effort split families and caused major disruptions in Indian communities.
The sections regarding band lists are in themselves discriminatory. Section 10 states:
Where the name of a male person is included in, omitted from, added to or deleted from a band list or general list, the names of his wife and his minor children shall also be included, omitted, added or deleted, as the case may be.
Does this section not have just as much built-in discrimination as section 12(l)(b)?
And what about section 12(b), which states:
The addition to a band list of the name of an illegitimate child may be protested at any time within 12 months after the addition, and if upon the protest it is decided that the father of the child was not an Indian, the child is not entitled to be registered.
Should we not be just as concerned about the rights of an illegitime child whose paternal antecedents it may be difficult to prove? These are but two examples of further discrimination within these clauses. If we were to examine the act clause by clause, many questions indeed similar to these would be raised.
The punitive and discriminatory clauses against Indian women and children might be more acceptable, or at least they might seem less unjust, if they were, in fact, a result of tribal custom or tradition, if it were a law that the Indians themselves had imposed. But it is not such a law. Rather it is a white man's law, imposed at white man's convenience, in order to encourage and speed up the process of assimilation of the Indian with the white man.
The Indian Act, as originally handed down in the late eighteen hundreds and subsequently amended, is based upon a patrilineal descent model. In this regard, the act may be seen as an extension of white Canadian colonial policy, for traditionally not all native peoples were organized along these lines. Iroquoian and many northwest coastal groups, for examples, emphasized matrilineal descent, and women in these societies maintained focal economic and political roles. By legislating these roles to males, the Indian Act represented, and continues to represent, imposition and interference by the federal government.
The process of assimilation of the Indians was seen by the settlers as a good thing. It was to Christianize and civilize them. Furthermore, the Indian women made good wives since they knew much more than the white men, such as how to survive the harsh conditions of the new country.

June 15, 1978
Indian Affairs
But that process of assimilation that was beneficial to the white settlers has not been beneficial to Indian communities. The traditional and essentially unchanged emphasis on family relationships in Indian communities must not be underestimated. Traditionally it is the Indian women who transmit Indian cultural values and language from one generation to the next. The enfranchisement of Indian women, the loss of their status, represents a great loss to the Indian community.
When this act was drawn up and even when it was amended, assimilation was the name of the game. Between its lines it is easy to sense the attitude of its framers, namely that in the long run it would be best for Indians to merge quietly into the rest of Canadian society. For example, section 15 of the present act provides a kind of lump sum payment to Indians who give up their legal status as such. That is not quite a bribe to deny their Indian identity, but it is certainly very close to one.
Many Indians in the past who opted for enfranchisement have done so without realizing the full consequences of their act. They did not realize that along with the lump sum payment went virtual banishment from the reserve and its amenities. It has become more and more obvious in recent years, as Indian groups have become more and more vocal about their rights and their heritage, that assimilation in white society and blind acceptance of white society's values is the last thing that the Indian wants.
It is time for the Indian Act to undergo total revision so that it can incorporate the desires and demands of the Indian community as to the kind of status they have in relation to the rest of Canadian society, and it must be spelled out clearly so all those who live under its mandate will be aware of all the consequences and implications of the various sections.
In this regard, it is indeed interesting to note what the advisory council's report has to say about the way in which the Indian Act is perceived by many Indians. It says and I quote: Indian Rights for Indian Women is at present considering options for a definition of membership which would replace the present discriminatory sections of the Indian Act. Their work is complicated by the fact that neither Indian women nor Indian men have much knowledge of the contents of the Indian Act, if indeed they have heard of it at all. Even if .they possess a copy of it, it is phrased in tortuous English which is very difficult to understand even if one's first language is English.
From 345 questionnaires administered by six native women researchers it was found that 49 per cent of both men and women had never heard of the Indian Act. Of the 51 per cent who had, less than half had ever read the act. Sixty-one per cent of the native people interviewed had a relative or close friend who had lost his or her Indian status and 86 per cent of these were through marriage, Only 16 per cent agreed with the present method of according status only through the male.
Considering how the Indian Act affects so many aspects of these people's lives, it is incredible that they should be allowed to remain in ignorance of its provisions. Can one picture the banking community being as ignorant of the Bank Act or as ignored in its drafting?
It is important that the needs and desires of the Indians themselves be taken into consideration in the review and 
redrafting of the Indian Act. That is what our proposed committee would do-solicit the views of the Indian community, including the women. This committee would deal with all aspects of the Indian Act, but especially those clauses which so blatantly discriminate against women. It would listen to the demands of the Indian women's organizations. So far these demands have been ignored. As the advisory council report points out:
To be born poor, an Indian and a female is to be a member of the most disadvantaged minority in Canada today, a citizen minus. It is to be victimized and utterly powerless, and to be, by government decree, without legal recourse of any kind.
That such a situation should exist in Canada today is appalling. We Canadians are often smug about such matters. We are prone to look down our noses at other countries where discimination is practised and to pretend that we are so tolerant. However, we can take no pride in our supposed tolerance so long as the blatant discrimination that is in the Indian Act remains on our statute books.
In removing those discriminatory sections of the act, and in seeking real input from the Indian community in the review and overhaul of the entire act, the committee that we are proposing would enhance our credibility as a nation concerned with human rights. If the committee did its work well, it might even begin to erode some of the distrust that the Indian community has felt toward the white man and his government for so long.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Milne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL JOINT COMMITTEE TO REVIEW PROVISIONS OF THE INDIAN ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak on the motion and comment on some of the viewpoints expressed by members opposite as well as to set out one or two ideas which I hold personally about revision of the Indian Act.
I feel strongly that to support the motion put forward by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes) would not be in the best interest of the parliamentary process or of the Indian people themselves. When speaking earlier this day, the minister said it was his view that it would be much more constructive and productive to set out some concrete proposals so that when they were referred to the committee, it could take positive action. That is the correct course and I, personally, very much endorse it.
The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) went to some length to take credit for having gotten the government to adopt the procedure whereby they established a committee to study the constitution. I draw to her attention that it is the procedure which the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Faulkner) is following in the constitutional question where some very specific proposals are being put forward for consideration.
If the process put forward by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent had been followed in the constitution, the whole process would not go very far. It would not be very effective and would not serve this House very well in addressing a badly needed subject. I just make the comment that I think the parallel is here.
June 15, 1978

The minister said earlier today that a number of areas have been identified with the Indian leadership where there is agreement in terms of revising the act, and that these can move forward. Indeed, the minister said it is hoped that by next year these can be put together in some form. Whether that form will be a bill, white paper, a series of proposals or whatever, at that point it would be referred to the committee. The committee would then have something useful to work with.
I would like to argue-and I am glad that my friend, the hon. member for Coast Chilcotin (Mr. Pearsall), who spoke earlier shares this view-that rather than have a special parliamentary committee consisting of members of this House and the other place, the proper committee would be the standing committee.
In discussing this with the Indian leadership, particularly the president of the National Indian Brotherhood, today, he drew to our attention that a good deal is required in the educational process before we can effectively deal with some of these matters, he has a very good point.
With regard to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development, those who have been members of that committee for four years or longer and regularly attend and participate are a good deal more effective than members who join it in the short term. They have had the opportunity to listen to many different points of view. In their duties, they have met many of the Indian leadership people, band chiefs and councils and have travelled to many of the reserves. There is a good deal of expertise in the standing committee. It would be better to refer the matter there than to establish a new committee.
It is good that the hon. member for Lambton-Kent has put this motion before us for debate. It has given members of all parties the opportunity to put forward their points of view on the revision on the Indian Act. In so doing, I thought a number of his colleagues would have had some positive and creative suggestions to offer in terms of revising the act rather than rehashing some of the old issues that may or may not be related to revising that act.
I would like to comment on some of the remarks made by members opposite in order to clear up the point about the fact that the minister was not following what was agreed to in the standing committee. I refer the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) and the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) to the proceedings of the standing committee for Thursday, May 4. While discussing the establishment of a committee, the chairman concluded the discussion by saying, and I quote:
I think we would have to have an order of the House, No. 1, referring the Annual Report; No. 2, authorizing us to engage additional staff; No. 3, allowing us to travel. But these are matters which would have to be discussed by the steering committee and I would suggest that we hold a meeting shortly for that purpose. Is that agreed?
The committee agreed to that. Out of the steering committee came agreement that if the estimates were terminated as has been scheduled, it would ask for a reference to the
Indian Affairs
standing committee of the annual report. If the time for consideration of the estimates was to be extended, it would not so ask. Therefore, no request to the House was made for a reference and that committee was never formulated.
Members opposite made a number of points regarding discrimination against Indian women. I do not want to in any way misquote the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, but I think he made the comment that this question was addressed mainly or specifically to discrimination in the act against Indian women. It is certainly the intention of the minister when contemplating revision of the act to consider the whole question of the rights of Indian men, women and children, matrimonial contracts, property laws and a number of related issues.
The hon. member for Kingston and The Islands spoke at some length on this question. I think she gave the impression that everyone in the Indian community was excited about the possibility that this process would be completed very quickly and that it would be simple. The issue is a good deal more complex than the hon. lady suggests and there is not unanimous agreement among the reserves with respect to it. One of the Indian leaders with whom I had a conversation earlier- she is in the gallery this evening-made the point that there is considerable opposition to it. The government would proceed very slowly and carefully on this question and consider it in the broadest context, rather than within the somewhat narrow limits which were set out during the debate.
The present act contains an almost unbelievable number of anachronisms which must date back a long way. Perhaps I might be allowed to put two or three examples on the record. Under section 32, for example, an Indian may not sell agricultural produce from a reserve in Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta without permission. The section reads:
A transaction of any kind whereby a band or any member thereof purports to sell, barter, exchange, give or otherwise dispose of cattle or other animals, grain or hay whether wild or cultivated or root crops or plants or other products from a reserve in Manitoba, Saskatchewan or Alberta to a person other than a member of that band is void unless the superintendent approves the transaction in writing.
Under section 120 an Indian child who does not attend school regularly become a juvenile delinquent. The section states:
An Indian child who is expelled or suspended from school or who refuses or fails to attend school regularly shall be deemed to be juvenile delinquent within the meaning of the Juvenile Delinquents Act.
There are many provisions of this type which need to be changed in order to bring the legislation more in keeping with the times and with the increased maturity of the Indian people.
I am somewhat concerned that so many of the contributions made in the debate today should have referred back to the white paper. Their intention seemed to be to make the point that revisions to the act would probably be a rehash of the white paper. Surely, from the minister's statement, it is apparent that the intention is completely the opposite. The intention is to give more authority to the band councils and to the elected people on the reserves so that they themselves can

June 15, 1978
Indian Affairs
make the decisions which affect their day to day operations, their cultural identity and the preservation of their culture.
It seems to me the thrust of the amendments will be in the opposite direction to that suggested by a number of speakers. It is a disservice to the process in which we are about to engage to rehash all the negative aspects of the white paper rather than look positively on the situation the government is creating through a new Indian Act.
I think it was the hon. member for Moose Jaw who quoted from a conversation with Chief Ahenakew a couple of years ago during which the chief said, in effect: "We don't want any handouts, we don't want any welfare because welfare is destroying our people; what we want is opportunity, encouragement, responsibility to make decisions on our own; we look to the future when native people would be self-reliant and able through their own endeavours to take care of themselves."
The hon. member then went on to discuss the shortcomings of the endeavours of the government to assist the Indian economy. Everyone is concerned about the low average income of the Indian people. I am sure all hon. members will support the efforts being made to improve that situation. The Indian economic development fund has certainly had its problems, but we should in fairness acknowledge that within the white business community there are substantial numbers of failures; not every project financed by the private sector is a success.
While there have been difficulties and some failures, there have also been a number of outstanding successes not only from a financial point of view but also from the point of view of increased confidence and experienced leadership developed as a result of this program. So I really think this has been one of the more positive of the department's undertakings. This is not to say that changes are not needed in the way the fund is administered or even in the concept of the fund. It seems to me it is important that members should think this issue through at the present time because there is a strong relationship between the future development of this project and the revisions to the act which are now being considered.
The minister, along with other members, commented on the Indian socio-economic development strategy report issued last December by the National Indian Brotherhood. This was really the product of extensive consultation within the Indian community across the country and it seems a number of revisions to the act would be required to meet its objectives. For one thing, there is certainly a need to clarify the status of legal contracts, whether, in fact, corporations would have full legal status, what is the legal position of corporations, whether they would have the right to sue Indian people involved in economic development where moneys are owing, and what rights Indian people enjoy before the courts. There is a direct relationship between all these questions and the revisions which, perhaps, should be made to the act to enable certain changes to be accomplished.
It seems to me one of the most welcome changes to the Indian Act is the one the minister mentioned today which would give the bands more authority to deal with land. I do not mean by that severances or surrender or outright sale, but
[Mr. Milne.)
certainly there might be opportunity for bands entering into economic development projects to set aside for a time parcels of land which could be used for equity purposes and, hopefully, draw in a much higher rate of private financing than has been available previously. In the private sector, once land is assembled, it is used as a basis for equity against borrowing. It is extremely difficult for Indians to do this under present procedures. If there were provision for negotiated agreements with the bands, the more mature bands would certainly be able to make decisions with regard to the type of economic development they wished to undertake. However, they will certainly need more control over the use of land than they have at the present time if land is to be considered an asset and key in terms of promoting better economic development.
What we are proposing in relation to legal status of bands and transfer of powers and responsibilities is something which extends beyond the notion of developing band government for Indian people. It is something which promises to reach to the heart of the social and economic development of the Indian people. Mr. Ahenakew has made a plea for Indian people to be provided the opportunity, encouragement and responsibility to make their own decisions, thereby becoming self-reliant and able through their own endeavours to take care of themselves. It is our job to make that possible. I am sure all hon. members in this House are dedicated to doing that in terms of leadership within the Indian community.
1 want to join other hon. members who have spoken in this debate in paying tribute to the leadership given to Canada through this government by the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand). He is the only Indian in the cabinet and, I believe, in the government.

Mr. Speaker, in the three minutes which are left to me there is little opportunity to discuss two other matters which are very vital parts of the Indian Act. Perhaps I should say they should be vital parts of the Indian Act or at least of Indian policy. The matters to which I am referring deal with housing and health.
I heard the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Milne) and of the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Penner). I heard them criticize the speeches which have been made today by hon. members of the official opposition, and I can only say that I am very disappointed. Because I have taken the time to listen to and to read the speech by the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), and I feel that his speech was on a very high and constructive level. The criticism he made was of a constructive nature. There was nothing in his speech which hit below the belt, a habit we see very frequently opposite.
It is my opinion-and it is shared by others-that the hon. member for Thunder Bay, who I suppose has periodically served on the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and
June 15, 1978

Northern Development and who has been parliamentary secretary to the minister, is probably still of the opinion that a potlatch is something to secure the lid of his Tupperware.
I was surprised at the remarks of the parliamentary secretary this evening. He said that he thinks perhaps some changes could be made here and that perhaps some changes could be made there. That is a clear indication of the thinking of this government. It is patchwork thinking in Indian affairs whether it deals with economic programs, social programs, health or housing. It is patchwork, make-work and ineffective.
